eras.name: Before the Nations
eras.power: No empire yet — clans and city-states
eras.captivity: None. Humanity is scattered, not enslaved.
rulers: Nimrod, first to build an empire (Gen 10:8–10)
eras.note: Creation, the Flood, and Babel. Josephus dates the whole stretch from Adam to Isaac at 3,833 years.

eras.name: The Patriarchs
eras.captivity: None — but the 400 years of bondage are foretold to Abram (Gen 15:13).
eras.note: One family walking through other people's kingdoms, owning nothing but a burial cave and a promise.

eras.name: Egypt and the Exodus
eras.captivity: EGYPTIAN BONDAGE. Israel is enslaved for generations under the pharaohs.
eras.note: The first captivity, and the pattern for every one after it: oppression, a cry, a deliverer, a covenant.

eras.name: The Wilderness
eras.power: Israel under Moses; no settled land
eras.captivity: Freed from Egypt, not yet in the land. A generation dies in the desert.
eras.note: Where the Law is given. Nearly every statute in the Bible is written in this forty-year window.

eras.name: The Conquest
eras.captivity: None. Israel is the invading power.
eras.note: Land is taken and divided by lot. The tribal map of the rest of the Old Testament is drawn here.

eras.name: The Judges
eras.power: No central government — 'every man did that which was right in his own eyes'
eras.captivity: SEVEN OPPRESSIONS in cycles: Mesopotamia, Moab, Canaan under Jabin, Midian, Ammon, and Philistia.
eras.note: Not a captivity in a foreign land but repeated subjugation at home. The book keeps count of the years.

eras.name: The United Kingdom
eras.power: Israel at its height; Egypt and Assyria both weak
eras.captivity: None. The nation is free, wealthy, and building.
eras.note: One throne over twelve tribes. The Temple is built. It lasts three reigns.

eras.name: The Divided Kingdom
eras.power: Two rival Hebrew kingdoms; Assyria rising
eras.captivity: None yet, but tribute and vassalage begin.
rulers: ISRAEL (north): Jeroboam I → Ahab → Jehu → Hoshea
eras.note: Ten tribes north under Jeroboam, two tribes south under Rehoboam. Most of the prophets speak into this split.

eras.name: The Assyrian Captivity
eras.captivity: THE TEN TRIBES ARE DEPORTED. Shalmaneser takes Samaria; the north never returns.
eras.note: Judah survives alone for another 130 years and watches what happened to its brother.

eras.name: The Babylonian Captivity
eras.captivity: JUDAH IS DEPORTED IN THREE WAVES (605, 597, 586). Jerusalem and the Temple are burned. Seventy years.
rulers: Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin and Zedekiah in Judah
eras.note: The exile that produced Ezekiel, Daniel and Lamentations — and the one Jeremiah had timed in advance.

eras.name: The Persian Return
eras.captivity: Ended by decree. Jews are free to return but remain a Persian province.
eras.note: Temple rebuilt, walls rebuilt, the Law read aloud in public. The Old Testament closes here.

eras.name: Greek Rule
eras.power: Macedon, then Ptolemaic Egypt and Seleucid Syria
eras.captivity: Occupation and forced Hellenization under Antiochus IV; brief independence under the Maccabees.
eras.note: No canonical book is written here — the four hundred silent years. Josephus is the main witness.

eras.name: Roman Rule
eras.captivity: Client kingdom, then direct rule by prefects. Jerusalem is destroyed again in AD 70.
eras.note: The Gospels, Acts and every letter in the New Testament are written under Roman power.

sections.note: Torah — the five books of Moses

sections.name: Poetry & Wisdom
sections.note: Songs, proverbs and the problem of suffering

sections.note: The long books of warning and promise

books.name: Genesis
books.full: The First Book of Moses: Called Genesis
books.scribe: Moses, by long tradition — working, most scholars think, from older family records and oral genealogies. The book itself names no author.
books.summary: The book of beginnings: world, humanity, sin, nations, and one family chosen out of them. It ends with that family safe in Egypt and a coffin waiting to be carried home.
prophecies: Gen 3:15 — the seed of the woman shall bruise the serpent's head
Gen 12:1–3 — in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed
Gen 15:13 — thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not theirs four hundred years
Gen 49:10 — the sceptre shall not depart from Judah
laws: The Sabbath pattern (2:2–3)
Bloodshed answerable to God (9:5–6)
Circumcision as covenant sign (17:10–14)
books.captivity: None yet — but foretold in chapter 15.

moves.n: Creation, fall, flood, Babel — the whole world in eleven chapters.
Called out of Ur, given a covenant, tested on a mountain.
A stolen blessing, twenty years in exile, a wrestling match, a new name.
Sold by his brothers into the empire that will one day enslave them all.

chapters.1: Six days of creation and a seventh of rest. The refrain 'and God saw that it was good' runs through it, and humanity is made in God's image, male and female, and given dominion.
chapters.2: The second account, from ground level: a garden, two named trees, a river in four heads, the naming of the animals, and the making of woman from the man's side.
chapters.3: The serpent, the fruit, the hiding, and the three sentences. Verse 15 — the seed of the woman bruising the serpent's head — is read as the first messianic promise in the Bible.
chapters.4: Cain and Abel. Two offerings, one murder, and a mark of protection on the killer. The chapter closes with Cain's line building the first city and inventing metalwork and music.
chapters.5: The genealogy from Adam to Noah, with ages. Enoch walks with God and is not, for God took him — the only break in the drumbeat of 'and he died'.
chapters.6: The sons of God, the giants, and God's grief that he had made man. Noah is told to build an ark to exact specifications and to take his household aboard.
chapters.7: The flood. Forty days of rain, the fountains of the deep broken up, and the waters prevailing on the earth a hundred and fifty days.
chapters.8: The waters recede. A raven, then a dove three times, and an olive leaf. Noah leaves the ark and builds an altar; God promises seedtime and harvest will not cease.
chapters.9: The covenant with all flesh, sealed by the rainbow. Blood is forbidden as food, and the shedding of human blood made answerable. Noah's drunkenness and the curse on Canaan follow.
chapters.10: The table of nations — seventy descendants of Shem, Ham and Japheth, mapped to peoples and territories. Nimrod appears as the first to be mighty on the earth and the founder of Babel and Nineveh.
chapters.11: The tower of Babel. One language, one plan, and a scattering. The chapter then narrows sharply from all nations to one man: Terah takes his son Abram out of Ur toward Canaan.
chapters.12: THE CALL. Get thee out of thy country, and I will make of thee a great nation — in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. Abram goes, and then goes down to Egypt and lies about his wife.
chapters.13: Abram and Lot separate over grazing rights. Lot chooses the well-watered plain toward Sodom; God restates the promise of the land to Abram, telling him to walk its length and breadth.
chapters.14: A war of four kings against five. Lot is taken captive and Abram rescues him with 318 trained men. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God, brings bread and wine and receives a tithe.
chapters.15: The covenant cut. Abram is told to count the stars, and he believed in the LORD, and he counted it to him for righteousness. He is also told his seed will be strangers in a land not theirs FOUR HUNDRED YEARS.
chapters.16: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, then despises her when she conceives. Hagar flees, meets the angel of the LORD at a well, and names him Thou God seest me. Ishmael is born.
chapters.17: Circumcision given as the sign of the covenant. Abram becomes Abraham and Sarai becomes Sarah; the promise of a son to a hundred-year-old man is made specific, and Abraham laughs.
chapters.18: Three visitors at Mamre. Sarah laughs behind the tent door and is questioned about it. Then Abraham bargains God down from fifty righteous men to ten over the fate of Sodom.
chapters.19: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. Lot is dragged out by the angels; his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. The chapter ends with the incest that produces Moab and Ammon.
chapters.20: Abraham repeats the lie about Sarah, this time to Abimelech of Gerar, who is warned in a dream and confronts him. Abraham's explanation is that she is in fact his half-sister.
chapters.21: Isaac is born and Sarah's laughter changes meaning. Hagar and Ishmael are sent away and rescued at a well, and Abraham makes a treaty with Abimelech at Beersheba.
chapters.22: THE BINDING OF ISAAC. Three days' walk, the wood carried by the son, the question about the lamb, and the ram caught in a thicket. God swears by himself to bless Abraham's seed.
chapters.23: Sarah dies at 127. Abraham negotiates publicly with the sons of Heth and pays four hundred shekels for the cave of Machpelah — the only land he ever owns in the country he was promised.
chapters.24: The longest chapter in Genesis: a servant sent to find Isaac a wife, a prayer at a well answered before he finishes it, Rebekah watering ten camels, and her decision to go.
chapters.25: Abraham dies and is buried by both sons. Then Esau and Jacob wrestle in the womb, and Esau sells his birthright for a bowl of red lentils because he is hungry.
chapters.26: Isaac's chapter — famine, the same lie about his wife, and a series of contested wells. God renews the covenant with him directly at Beersheba.
chapters.27: The stolen blessing. Goatskins on the hands, venison substituted, and a blind father deceived. Esau's cry is that his brother has now taken both birthright and blessing; Jacob runs.
chapters.28: Jacob sleeps with a stone for a pillow at Bethel and sees a ladder set up on the earth reaching to heaven. God repeats the promise to him, and he makes a conditional vow.
chapters.29: Jacob meets Rachel at the well and serves seven years for her, which seemed to him but a few days. Laban substitutes Leah in the dark, and he serves seven more.
chapters.30: The birth contest between two sisters and two handmaids produces eleven sons and a daughter. Then Jacob's speckled-and-spotted breeding scheme turns Laban's flocks into his own.
chapters.31: Jacob flees with his family and herds. Rachel steals her father's household gods and sits on them. Laban catches up; they build a stone heap as a boundary neither will cross.
chapters.32: Jacob wrestles a man until daybreak at Peniel, refuses to let go without a blessing, and is renamed ISRAEL. He limps away, and Esau is coming with four hundred men.
chapters.33: The brothers meet. Esau runs, embraces him, and weeps; the feared reckoning never comes. Jacob sends the gifts anyway and settles at Shechem.
chapters.34: Dinah is violated at Shechem. Simeon and Levi use circumcision as a trap and kill every male in the city while they are recovering — an act Jacob is still condemning on his deathbed.
chapters.35: Back to Bethel: idols buried under an oak, the name Israel confirmed, Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac is buried by both his sons.
chapters.36: The generations of Esau — the dukes and kings of Edom. A whole chapter given to the brother who is not the line, listing kings that reigned before any king reigned in Israel.
chapters.37: Joseph's coat, his two dreams, and his brothers' response. Sold to Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver, and a coat dipped in goat's blood carried back to his father.
chapters.38: The interruption: Judah and Tamar. A widow denied her legal right takes it by disguise, and Judah admits she has been more righteous than he. Their son Pharez appears in David's genealogy.
chapters.39: Joseph in Potiphar's house — trusted with everything, propositioned daily, and jailed on a false charge. The refrain is that the LORD was with him, even in prison.
chapters.40: Two dreams in prison: the butler restored, the baker hanged. Joseph asks to be remembered, and the butler forgets him for two full years.
chapters.41: Pharaoh's two dreams. Joseph is shaved and brought from the dungeon, interprets seven fat and seven lean years, proposes a grain policy, and is made second in Egypt at thirty.
chapters.42: The brothers come to buy corn and bow, fulfilling the dream. Joseph accuses them of spying, keeps Simeon, and returns their money secretly. Guilt surfaces in their conversation.
chapters.43: The second journey with Benjamin. Judah pledges himself as surety. Joseph seats them in birth order, which unnerves them, and gives Benjamin five times the portion.
chapters.44: The silver cup planted in Benjamin's sack. Judah, who once sold Joseph, offers to become a slave in his brother's place — the moment the test is designed to produce.
chapters.45: Joseph makes himself known, weeping so loudly the Egyptians hear. Ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good. Wagons are sent to bring the whole family down.
chapters.46: Jacob offers sacrifice at Beersheba and is told not to fear going to Egypt. Seventy souls are listed by name, and Joseph meets his father's chariot at Goshen.
chapters.47: Jacob blesses Pharaoh. The famine deepens and Joseph nationalises Egypt's land and livestock, instituting a fifth to Pharaoh — leaving only the priests' land untouched.
chapters.48: Jacob adopts Joseph's two sons as his own and crosses his hands deliberately, putting the younger Ephraim ahead of Manasseh over Joseph's objection.
chapters.49: Jacob's blessings on the twelve tribes, in poetry. Judah is given the lion and the sceptre, with the line that it shall not depart from him until Shiloh come.
chapters.50: Jacob is embalmed in Egypt and carried to Machpelah. The brothers fear reprisal; Joseph reassures them, makes Israel swear to carry his bones up, and the book ends with a coffin in Egypt.

books.name: Exodus
books.full: The Second Book of Moses: Called Exodus
books.scribe: Moses. Ex 24:4 records that he wrote the words of the LORD, and 17:14 that he wrote in a book by command.
rulers: The pharaoh who knew not Joseph
books.summary: Israel goes from brickyard to covenant nation in one generation. Ten plagues break Egypt's grip, the sea opens, and at Sinai a company of freed slaves is given a law and a tabernacle.
prophecies: Ex 3:12 — ye shall serve God upon this mountain
Ex 12:14 — the Passover kept as a memorial for ever
laws: The Ten Commandments (20:1–17)
The Book of the Covenant — civil law (21–23)
Passover and unleavened bread (12)
Tabernacle, priesthood and Sabbath (25–31)
books.captivity: EGYPTIAN BONDAGE — broken in chapter 12.

moves.n: A new pharaoh, a basket in the river, a burning bush.
Each one strikes an Egyptian god; the last one takes the firstborn.
The sea, the manna, the water from the rock, Jethro's advice.
The Ten Commandments and the Book of the Covenant.
Detailed specifications given on the mountain.
Broken tablets, intercession, a second set.
The glory fills it, and the book stops.

chapters.1: Four centuries pass in a paragraph. A new king who knew not Joseph sets taskmasters over Israel; the midwives Shiphrah and Puah refuse the order to kill.
chapters.2: An ark of bulrushes among the flags. Moses kills an Egyptian, is rebuked by a Hebrew, and flees to Midian, where he waters Jethro's daughters' flock.
chapters.3: The bush that burns without being consumed, and the ground made holy. Moses asks for a name and is given I AM THAT I AM.
chapters.4: Three signs: the rod that becomes a serpent, the leprous hand, water turned to blood. Moses pleads a slow tongue; Aaron is given him as a mouth.
chapters.5: The first audience with Pharaoh makes everything worse — bricks without straw, and the officers beaten. Moses complains to God about it.
chapters.6: The answer: I appeared unto Abraham as God Almighty, but by my name JEHOVAH was I not known to them. A genealogy interrupts the narrative.
chapters.7: Aaron's rod swallows the magicians' rods. The first plague turns the river to blood, and the magicians match it.
chapters.8: Frogs, lice and flies. The magicians fail at the lice and call it the finger of God. Pharaoh begins bargaining and reneging.
chapters.9: Murrain on cattle, boils the magicians cannot stand before, and hail that spares Goshen. Pharaoh admits he has sinned, then hardens again.
chapters.10: Locusts, and a darkness that may be felt for three days. Pharaoh offers to let the men go, then everyone but the flocks.
chapters.11: The last plague announced. The Israelites are told to ask their neighbours for jewels of silver and gold.
chapters.12: The Passover instituted with the lamb, the blood on the lintel, and unleavened bread. They go out at night, 430 years to the day.
chapters.13: The firstborn set apart, and the feast kept as a sign upon the hand. The pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.
chapters.14: The sea divided by an east wind all that night. Israel goes over on dry ground; the Egyptians follow and the waters return.
chapters.15: The song of Moses and Miriam with her timbrel — among the oldest poetry in the Bible. Three days later they find bitter water at Marah.
chapters.16: Manna, described as small and round like coriander seed. A double portion on the sixth day, and none on the seventh.
chapters.17: Water from the rock at Horeb. Amalek attacks, and Israel prevails while Moses' hands are held up by Aaron and Hur.
chapters.18: Jethro watches Moses judge from morning to evening and tells him it is not good. Rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens are appointed.
chapters.19: Sinai in the third month. Bounds set about the mount, thunders and lightnings, and a trumpet exceeding loud.
chapters.20: The Ten Commandments. The people stand afar off and ask that God speak to them through Moses instead.
chapters.21: The judgments begin: Hebrew servants and the ear bored to the door, then laws of violence, and the ox that gores.
chapters.22: Restitution for theft and damage, and protection for the stranger, the widow and the fatherless.
chapters.23: Justice not to follow a multitude to do evil. Three annual feasts, the sabbath year, and an angel sent before them.
chapters.24: The covenant sealed with blood sprinkled on the people. Seventy elders see the God of Israel and eat and drink; Moses goes up for forty days.
chapters.25: The pattern shown in the mount: the ark with its mercy seat and cherubim, the table of shewbread, and the lampstand of beaten gold.
chapters.26: The tabernacle itself — ten curtains of fine twined linen, boards of shittim wood, and the veil dividing the holy from the most holy.
chapters.27: The brasen altar with its horns, the court with its hangings, and oil olive beaten for the lamp to burn always.
chapters.28: The priestly garments for glory and for beauty: the ephod, the breastplate with twelve stones, the Urim and Thummim, and bells on the hem.
chapters.29: The seven-day consecration of Aaron and his sons — washing, robing, anointing, and blood on the ear, thumb and toe.
chapters.30: The altar of incense, the ransom of half a shekel, the laver of brass, and the anointing oil that may not be copied.
chapters.31: Bezaleel and Aholiab named and filled with the Spirit for craftsmanship. The sabbath given as a sign. Then the two tables of stone.
chapters.32: The golden calf, made while Moses is still on the mountain. The tables broken at the foot of it, and Moses offering to be blotted out instead.
chapters.33: The tent pitched outside the camp, where God speaks to Moses face to face. Shew me thy glory — answered with a cleft in the rock.
chapters.34: Two new tables. The proclamation of the name: merciful and gracious, longsuffering. Moses comes down with his face shining and veils it.
chapters.35: The sabbath repeated, then a call for freewill offerings. The people bring bracelets, earrings, spun goats' hair and badgers' skins.
chapters.36: The craftsmen have to be restrained — the people bring much more than enough for the work, and are told to stop.
chapters.37: Bezaleel makes the ark, the table, the lampstand and the incense altar, exactly to the pattern given in chapter 25.
chapters.38: The altar, the laver made from the women's looking glasses, and the court. An inventory of all the metal used.
chapters.39: The garments finished, and the whole work brought to Moses, who looks upon it and blesses them.
chapters.40: The tabernacle reared on the first day of the first year. The cloud covers it and the glory fills it, so that Moses cannot enter.

books.name: Leviticus
books.full: The Third Book of Moses: Called Leviticus
books.scribe: Moses. The book is framed as direct dictation — 'and the LORD spake unto Moses, saying' opens most chapters.
rulers: Aaron and his sons as the first priesthood
books.summary: A manual for living next door to a holy God. Sacrifice, priesthood, clean and unclean, festival calendar, and the year of jubilee.
prophecies: Lev 26 — blessings for obedience and a sevenfold chastening, ending in exile among the nations
laws: Five offerings (1–7)
Clean and unclean (11–15)
Day of Atonement (16)
'Love thy neighbour as thyself' (19:18)
Feasts of the LORD (23)
Sabbath year and jubilee (25)
books.power: None — Israel is encamped at Sinai
books.captivity: Free, unsettled.

moves.n: Burnt, meat, peace, sin and trespass — what each is for.
And Nadab and Abihu killed for strange fire.
Food, childbirth, skin disease, discharge.
One day a year, one man, two goats.
Sexual law, neighbour law, priestly conduct.
Feasts, the sabbath year, and the jubilee.
Terms of the covenant, including exile.

chapters.1: The burnt offering, wholly consumed. Herd, flock or fowl, so that the poor are not excluded.
chapters.2: The meat offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense, without leaven or honey, seasoned with salt.
chapters.3: The peace offering, the one sacrifice partly eaten by the worshipper. The fat belongs to the LORD.
chapters.4: The sin offering, graded by who sinned — priest, congregation, ruler, common person — and always for sins done in ignorance.
chapters.5: The trespass offering, covering concealed knowledge, unclean contact and rash oaths, with a sliding scale down to two turtledoves.
chapters.6: Restitution for defrauding a neighbour, plus a fifth. The fire on the altar is to be kept burning and never go out.
chapters.7: The priests' portions defined. Two absolute prohibitions: no fat and no blood.
chapters.8: The consecration of chapter 29 carried out, over seven days, with the congregation gathered at the door.
chapters.9: On the eighth day Aaron offers for the first time. Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the offering; the people shout and fall.
chapters.10: Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire and are consumed. Aaron holds his peace. Priests are forbidden wine before serving.
chapters.11: Clean and unclean creatures: what parts the hoof and chews the cud, what has fins and scales. Ye shall be holy, for I am holy.
chapters.12: Purification after childbirth, and the offering of a lamb or, if she cannot afford it, two birds — the offering Mary brings in Luke 2.
chapters.13: The examination of leprosy in skin, hair, garments. The priest's role is diagnostic: shut up seven days, then look again.
chapters.14: The cleansing of a healed leper, with two birds, one killed and one let loose into the open field. Then leprosy in a house.
chapters.15: Bodily discharges and the uncleanness they carry — the background to the woman with the issue of blood in the Gospels.
chapters.16: The Day of Atonement. Two goats: one killed, one sent into the wilderness bearing the iniquities. Once a year, and not without blood.
chapters.17: All slaughter brought to the door of the tabernacle. The life of the flesh is in the blood, which is why it is not to be eaten.
chapters.18: Forbidden degrees of relation, and the practices of Egypt and Canaan. The land itself is said to vomit out its inhabitants.
chapters.19: The heart of the holiness code. Gleanings left for the poor, no respect of persons in judgment, and love thy neighbour as thyself.
chapters.20: Penalties attached to chapters 18 and 19, including Molech worship and consulting familiar spirits.
chapters.21: Restrictions on the priests: whom they may mourn, whom they may marry, and what blemishes disqualify from serving.
chapters.22: Offerings must be without blemish, and the priests must be clean to eat the holy things.
chapters.23: The feasts set out in order: sabbath, passover, unleavened bread, firstfruits, weeks, trumpets, atonement, tabernacles.
chapters.24: Oil for the lamps and twelve loaves of shewbread. Then a man blasphemes and is stoned, with the law of like for like attached.
chapters.25: The sabbath year and the jubilee. Land is not sold for ever, because the land is mine, and ye are strangers and sojourners with me.
chapters.26: Blessings for obedience and a long escalating list of curses — four rounds of sevenfold chastisement, ending in exile and yet remembrance.
chapters.27: Vows, valuations of persons and property, and the tithe. The book ends on redemption prices rather than on ceremony.

books.name: Numbers
books.full: The Fourth Book of Moses: Called Numbers
books.scribe: Moses. Num 33:2 says he wrote down the stages of the journey by command.
books.summary: Two censuses bracket forty years of wandering. A generation refuses the land at Kadesh and is buried in the desert; their children are counted and led to the edge of Jordan.
prophecies: Num 24:17 — there shall come a Star out of Jacob (Balaam's oracle)
laws: Nazarite vow (6)
Priestly blessing (6:24–26)
Cities of refuge (35)
Inheritance for daughters (27, 36)
books.captivity: Free, wandering.

moves.n: The camp organised tribe by tribe around the tabernacle.
Twelve spies, two good reports, forty years of consequence.
A revolt against Moses, Aaron's rod that budded.
Water from the rock, the bronze serpent, Balaam's oracles.
A new generation counted, land assigned, cities of refuge set.

chapters.1: A census of men able to go to war, taken in the wilderness of Sinai in the second year. The Levites are not numbered with them.
chapters.2: The camp arranged in four blocks of three tribes, each under its own standard, with the tabernacle in the middle.
chapters.3: The Levites given to Aaron, and numbered as a substitute for the firstborn of Israel, with the surplus redeemed at five shekels.
chapters.4: The duties of Kohath, Gershon and Merari for carrying the tabernacle. Kohath bears the holy things but may not look on them.
chapters.5: The unclean put outside the camp, restitution with a fifth, and the ordeal of bitter water for a wife suspected of unfaithfulness.
chapters.6: The Nazarite vow — no wine, no razor, no dead body. Then the Aaronic blessing: the LORD bless thee and keep thee.
chapters.7: The offerings of the twelve princes at the dedication, listed one by one on twelve successive days, identical each time.
chapters.8: The lamps set to give light in front of the lampstand. The Levites cleansed and offered as a wave offering.
chapters.9: A second Passover for those unclean or on a journey. The cloud on the tabernacle governs when they move and when they stay.
chapters.10: Two silver trumpets for assembly and for journeying. The camp sets out for the first time; Moses asks Hobab to be their eyes.
chapters.11: Complaining about manna and remembering the fish of Egypt freely. Seventy elders receive the Spirit; quails come with a plague.
chapters.12: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over his Ethiopian wife. Miriam becomes leprous and is shut out seven days.
chapters.13: Twelve spies sent from Kadesh. Ten report giants and walled cities; Caleb says we are well able to overcome it.
chapters.14: The people propose returning to Egypt. Forty years in the wilderness, a year for a day. Those who then try to go up are beaten back.
chapters.15: Offerings for when they come into the land — placed here deliberately. A sabbath-breaker stoned, and fringes with a ribband of blue.
chapters.16: Korah, Dathan and Abiram challenge Moses' authority. The earth opens; fire consumes the two hundred and fifty censers.
chapters.17: Twelve rods laid up overnight. Aaron's buds, blossoms and yields almonds, settling the question of priesthood.
chapters.18: The priests' and Levites' portions, since they have no inheritance in the land. The tithe of the tithe.
chapters.19: The red heifer burned outside the camp, and the water of separation made from its ashes for cleansing after contact with the dead.
chapters.20: Miriam dies at Kadesh. Moses strikes the rock twice instead of speaking to it and is barred from the land. Aaron dies on mount Hor.
chapters.21: The brazen serpent lifted on a pole. Victories over Sihon and Og, and a fragment quoted from the book of the wars of the LORD.
chapters.22: Balak hires Balaam. The ass sees the angel three times and finally speaks; Balaam is told to say only what he is given.
chapters.23: Two oracles from two hilltops. How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? Balak keeps moving him to a new view.
chapters.24: Balaam no longer seeks enchantments. The third and fourth oracles — how goodly are thy tents, and a Star out of Jacob.
chapters.25: Israel joins itself to Baal-peor. Phinehas ends the plague with a javelin and is given a covenant of peace.
chapters.26: A second census on the plains of Moab. Of the generation counted in chapter 1, only Caleb and Joshua remain.
chapters.27: The daughters of Zelophehad win the right to inherit. Joshua is set before Eleazar and given a charge in the sight of all.
chapters.28: The daily, sabbath, monthly and festival offerings set out as a calendar of what the nation owes.
chapters.29: The offerings of the seventh month — trumpets, atonement, and the descending count of bullocks through the feast of tabernacles.
chapters.30: The law of vows, and the conditions under which a father or husband may disallow one on the day he hears it.
chapters.31: The war on Midian, the division of the spoil, and the purification of everything that abides the fire.
chapters.32: Reuben and Gad want the cattle country east of Jordan. They may have it on condition they cross over armed and fight first.
chapters.33: The stages of the journey listed from Rameses to the plains of Moab — forty-two encampments, written down by Moses.
chapters.34: The borders of the land defined, and the men named who are to divide it.
chapters.35: Forty-eight cities for the Levites, six of them cities of refuge, with the distinction between murder and accident carefully drawn.
chapters.36: A follow-up to chapter 27: heiresses must marry within their own tribe so that no inheritance moves from tribe to tribe.

books.name: Deuteronomy
books.full: The Fifth Book of Moses: Called Deuteronomy
books.scribe: Moses, as recorded sermons on the plains of Moab; the account of his death in chapter 34 was added by another hand, traditionally Joshua.
books.summary: Moses preaches the law a second time to the generation that will actually cross. It is a covenant document: history, stipulations, witnesses, blessings and curses.
prophecies: Deut 18:15 — a Prophet like unto me shall the LORD raise up
Deut 28 — curses that name siege, deportation and scattering among all nations
Deut 30:1–5 — and the LORD will gather thee from all the nations
laws: The Shema (6:4–9)
Law of the king (17:14–20)
Test of a true prophet (18:20–22)
Release of debts every seventh year (15)
books.captivity: Free — with exile written into the covenant as a warning.

moves.n: What God has already done — forty years reviewed.
The law restated: the Shema, the king, the prophet, the courts.
Read aloud from two mountains; exile named as the endpoint.
Moses' song, his blessing, and his unmarked grave.

chapters.1: Moses begins the retrospect on the far side of Jordan. The appointment of judges, and the failure at Kadesh forty years earlier.
chapters.2: Edom, Moab and Ammon are passed by — their lands are not Israel's to take. Then Sihon is defeated.
chapters.3: Og of Bashan and his iron bedstead. Moses asks to cross over and is told to speak no more of that matter.
chapters.4: The first great exhortation. Ye saw no manner of similitude, therefore make no graven image. The cities of refuge east of Jordan set apart.
chapters.5: The Ten Commandments repeated, with the sabbath grounded in the deliverance from Egypt rather than in creation.
chapters.6: Hear, O Israel: the Shema. Love the LORD with all thine heart, and teach these words to thy children when thou sittest in thine house.
chapters.7: The seven nations to be driven out, with no covenant and no intermarriage. Israel is chosen not for numbers but because it was the fewest.
chapters.8: Remember the forty years. Man doth not live by bread only. The danger named is prosperity, and saying my power got me this wealth.
chapters.9: Not for thy righteousness. The golden calf, Massah, Taberah and Kibroth-hattaavah are all recalled against any self-congratulation.
chapters.10: The second tables and the ark. What doth the LORD require of thee, but to fear him and to love him and to serve him.
chapters.11: The land that drinks water of the rain of heaven, unlike Egypt watered by foot. The blessing and curse set on Gerizim and Ebal.
chapters.12: Worship centralised in the place the LORD shall choose. Sacrifice is restricted; ordinary slaughter for food is not.
chapters.13: The prophet whose sign comes true but who says let us go after other gods. The test is not the wonder but where it leads.
chapters.14: Clean and unclean creatures again, and the tithe, including the provision to turn it into money for a long journey and spend it there.
chapters.15: The seventh year of release, and the Hebrew servant freed with a liberal provision. Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy poor brother.
chapters.16: The three pilgrim feasts, then judges and officers in all the gates: that which is altogether just shalt thou follow.
chapters.17: The law of the king, written centuries before there was one — he shall not multiply horses, wives or silver, and shall write out a copy of the law.
chapters.18: The priests' portion, the prohibition of divination, and the promise of a Prophet like unto me, whom the New Testament repeatedly cites.
chapters.19: Three cities of refuge, with three more if the border extends. Landmarks not to be removed, and false witnesses judged as they intended.
chapters.20: Rules of war: exemptions for a new house, a new vineyard, a new wife, and the fearful. Fruit trees are not to be cut down for siege works.
chapters.21: The unsolved murder and the heifer in the valley. The rights of a firstborn by an unloved wife, and a body not left hanging overnight.
chapters.22: Lost property returned, roof parapets, unequal yokes, mixed seed and cloth, and a series of laws on marriage and sexual offences.
chapters.23: Who may enter the congregation, camp sanitation, escaped slaves not returned, and no usury from a brother.
chapters.24: The bill of divorcement, the millstone not taken in pledge, wages paid before sundown, and gleanings left for the stranger.
chapters.25: Forty stripes save one, the levirate duty and the loosed shoe, and just weights: thou shalt have a perfect and just measure.
chapters.26: The basket of firstfruits, brought with the confession that begins A Syrian ready to perish was my father.
chapters.27: The stones plastered and inscribed on mount Ebal, and twelve curses to which all the people say Amen.
chapters.28: Fourteen verses of blessing and fifty-four of curse, ending in siege, exile and a return to Egypt in ships. Quoted throughout the prophets.
chapters.29: The covenant made in the land of Moab, addressed also to him that is not here with us this day. The secret things belong unto the LORD.
chapters.30: The promise of return even after exile, and the choice set out plainly: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing.
chapters.31: Joshua commissioned, the law written and given to the priests, and a command to read it publicly every seventh year.
chapters.32: The Song of Moses, taught as a witness. The Rock, his work is perfect. Then Moses is told to go up mount Nebo and die there.
chapters.33: The blessing of the tribes, one by one. The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms.
chapters.34: Moses sees the land from Pisgah and dies in the land of Moab. No man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.

books.name: Joshua
books.scribe: Joshua for most of it (24:26 says he wrote these words in the book of the law); the closing verses about his death by a later scribe.
books.summary: The land is entered, fought for, and divided by lot. Jericho falls, Ai is lost and won, and the tribes receive borders that will define them for a thousand years.
prophecies: Josh 6:26 — a curse on the man who rebuilds Jericho, fulfilled in 1 Kgs 16:34
laws: Cities of refuge assigned (20)
Levitical cities (21)
books.captivity: None — Israel is the invading force.

moves.n: Jordan stopped, twelve stones, circumcision, the manna ceases.
Jericho, Achan's theft, Ai, Gibeon's trick, the long day.
Borders by lot, Levitical cities, cities of refuge.
An altar nearly starts a civil war; Joshua's last charge at Shechem.

chapters.1: The commission after Moses' death. Be strong and of a good courage, said three times, with the book of the law to be meditated on day and night.
chapters.2: Two spies in Rahab's house on the wall. The scarlet line in the window, and her confession that the land's courage has already melted.
chapters.3: The priests carry the ark into Jordan at flood stage, and the waters stand and rise up upon an heap.
chapters.4: Twelve stones taken from the riverbed and set up at Gilgal, so that children asking what these stones mean will be told.
chapters.5: A new generation circumcised, the reproach of Egypt rolled away, and the manna ceasing. The captain of the host of the LORD with a drawn sword.
chapters.6: Jericho: six days of silent circuit, then seven circuits and a shout. Rahab's household is brought out alive.
chapters.7: Defeat at Ai traced to Achan's Babylonish garment and wedge of gold hidden in his tent. Israel loses because one man took the accursed thing.
chapters.8: Ai taken by ambush. Then the whole law read at Ebal and Gerizim, with the strangers standing among them.
chapters.9: The Gibeonites arrive in mouldy bread and clouted shoes. Israel makes a league without asking counsel of the LORD, and is bound by its oath.
chapters.10: Five kings besiege Gibeon. Hailstones, and the sun standing still upon Gibeon — quoted from the book of Jasher.
chapters.11: The northern coalition under Jabin of Hazor. Chariots burned and horses houghed, since Israel is not to depend on them.
chapters.12: A list of thirty-one defeated kings, east and west of Jordan — an inventory rather than a narrative.
chapters.13: Joshua is old, and much land remains unpossessed. The eastern tribes' allotments are recorded.
chapters.14: Caleb at eighty-five asks for the hill country and the giants on it: give me this mountain.
chapters.15: Judah's border in detail, and Achsah asking her father for springs of water as well as a south land.
chapters.16: Ephraim's portion, with the note that they did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer.
chapters.17: Manasseh, and the daughters of Zelophehad receiving what Numbers promised them. The tribe complains its portion is too small.
chapters.18: The tabernacle set up at Shiloh. Seven tribes still have nothing, so men are sent to survey the land and describe it in a book.
chapters.19: The remaining allotments, ending with Joshua's own portion — taken last, not first.
chapters.20: The six cities of refuge appointed by name, three on each side of Jordan.
chapters.21: Forty-eight cities given to the Levites. Not one word failed of all that the LORD had spoken.
chapters.22: The eastern tribes build an altar by Jordan and are nearly attacked for it. It turns out to be a witness, not a rival, and is named Ed.
chapters.23: Joshua's first farewell, warning against alliances and intermarriage with the nations that remain.
chapters.24: At Shechem, the whole history rehearsed and the choice put: choose you this day. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

books.name: Judges
books.scribe: Traditionally Samuel, compiling older accounts. The refrain 'in those days there was no king in Israel' shows it was written after the monarchy began.
books.summary: Seven cycles of the same story: Israel forgets, is oppressed by a neighbouring power, cries out, is rescued by a judge, and forgets again. Each deliverer is rougher than the last.
books.captivity: SEVEN OPPRESSIONS: Mesopotamia 8 yrs, Moab 18, Jabin of Canaan 20, Midian 7, Ammon 18, Philistia 40.

moves.n: Incomplete conquest, and the cycle explained in advance.
The early judges; Deborah and Barak against Sisera.
Three hundred men with trumpets — then Abimelech's murderous kingship.
A rash vow and a man who never keeps one.
Two horror stories showing what 'no king in Israel' actually meant.

chapters.1: After Joshua's death, tribe by tribe, a record of what was not taken. The refrain is 'did not drive out'.
chapters.2: The angel at Bochim, and the pattern stated plainly — a generation arose which knew not the LORD. Sin, servitude, supplication, salvation, repeat.
chapters.3: Othniel, then Ehud with his dagger of a cubit length and left-handed thrust at Eglon, then Shamgar and his ox goad.
chapters.4: Deborah judging under her palm tree, Barak refusing to go without her, and Jael with a tent nail and a hammer.
chapters.5: The Song of Deborah, one of the oldest poems in the Bible — the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.
chapters.6: Gideon threshing wheat by the winepress, called a mighty man of valour. The altar of Baal pulled down, then the fleece twice.
chapters.7: Thirty-two thousand reduced to three hundred by the way they drank. Trumpets, pitchers and lamps, and a barley cake dream.
chapters.8: Zebah and Zalmunna pursued. Gideon refuses kingship, then makes an ephod of the golden earrings, and Israel goes a whoring after it.
chapters.9: Abimelech kills seventy brothers on one stone. Jotham's parable of the trees choosing a bramble. A millstone ends it.
chapters.10: Tola and Jair, then oppression by the Philistines and Ammon, and a repentance God at first refuses.
chapters.11: Jephthah the outcast made captain, and the vow about whatsoever cometh forth of the doors of my house — which turns out to be his daughter.
chapters.12: Ephraim quarrels again and is caught at the fords by their pronunciation of Shibboleth. Forty-two thousand fall.
chapters.13: The angel to Manoah's wife announcing Samson, with the Nazarite conditions given before his birth.
chapters.14: The lion and the honey, and a riddle wagered at a seven-day wedding feast that his wife weeps out of him.
chapters.15: Three hundred foxes with firebrands, and a thousand men killed with the jawbone of an ass at a place named for it.
chapters.16: The gates of Gaza carried uphill, then Delilah and four attempts. Eyes put out, grinding in the prison house, and the pillars.
chapters.17: Micah's household shrine and his hired Levite. Every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
chapters.18: The Danites, looking for territory, take Micah's idols and his priest as well, and settle at Laish.
chapters.19: The Levite's concubine at Gibeah — the darkest chapter in the book, ending with a body divided into twelve pieces.
chapters.20: The tribes gather against Benjamin. Two defeats, then an ambush, and Benjamin nearly wiped out.
chapters.21: Wives found for the six hundred survivors by two grim expedients. The book ends: there was no king in Israel.

books.name: Ruth
books.scribe: Unknown; traditionally Samuel. Written down after David, since the book ends by tracing his line.
books.written: c. 1000 BC, about events during the judges
books.summary: A famine, a widow, and a foreign woman who refuses to go home. Set in the worst period of the Old Testament, it is a quiet story about loyalty and legal redemption — and it ends with David's grandfather.
prophecies: Ruth 4:17–22 — the genealogy that runs to David, and through him to Christ
laws: Levirate marriage and the kinsman-redeemer (Deut 25:5–10, worked out in Ruth 4)
Gleaning rights for the poor and the stranger (Lev 19:9–10, seen in Ruth 2)
books.captivity: Local oppressions ongoing.

moves.n: Famine, migration, three deaths, and Ruth's refusal to go back.
Ruth ends up in the field of a kinsman by apparent accident.
Naomi's plan; Ruth asks Boaz to act as redeemer.
A sandal changes hands at the gate; a genealogy runs to David.

chapters.1: Famine, Moab, and three widows. Orpah goes back; Ruth says whither thou goest, I will go. Naomi returns and asks to be called Mara.
chapters.2: Ruth gleans, by chance, in the field of Boaz — a near kinsman, who tells the reapers to let handfuls fall on purpose.
chapters.3: Naomi's plan at the threshingfloor. Ruth asks Boaz to spread his skirt over her, and he names a nearer kinsman who must be asked first.
chapters.4: The transaction at the gate, sealed by drawing off a shoe. The genealogy at the end runs to David.

books.name: 1 Samuel
books.scribe: Samuel for the early chapters; Nathan and Gad are named in 1 Chr 29:29 as recorders of the rest.
rulers: David, anointed but not yet reigning
books.summary: Israel demands a king so as to be like the other nations. They get Saul, who begins well and unravels; and behind him a shepherd from Bethlehem is quietly anointed.
prophecies: 1 Sam 2:35 — I will raise me up a faithful priest
1 Sam 15:28 — the kingdom rent from Saul and given to a better man
laws: The manner of the king — what a monarchy will cost (8:11–18)
books.captivity: Philistine oppression; the ark itself is captured.

moves.n: Hannah's vow, the boy in the temple, the ark captured and returned.
Israel demands a king; Saul is chosen, then rejected twice over.
Anointed in secret, Goliath, Jonathan's friendship, Saul's spear.
David a fugitive; Saul dies on Gilboa with his sons.

chapters.1: Hannah praying at Shiloh so silently that Eli thinks her drunk. Samuel is born and lent to the LORD.
chapters.2: Hannah's song, which Mary's Magnificat echoes. Eli's sons take the meat by force; a man of God pronounces against the house.
chapters.3: The word of the LORD was precious in those days. Samuel called three times and answering to Eli before he learns whose voice it is.
chapters.4: The ark carried into battle as a talisman and captured. Eli falls backward and dies; a child is named Ichabod.
chapters.5: The ark in Dagon's temple. The idol falls twice, the second time with head and hands broken off upon the threshold.
chapters.6: The Philistines send the ark back on a new cart drawn by two milch kine, with golden emerods and mice as a trespass offering.
chapters.7: Samuel judges at Mizpeh and sets up a stone: Ebenezer, hitherto hath the LORD helped us.
chapters.8: Samuel's sons take bribes, and the elders ask for a king like all the nations. The manner of the king is spelled out as a warning.
chapters.9: Saul out looking for his father's lost asses, and a servant's suggestion that they consult the seer.
chapters.10: Saul anointed privately, then chosen publicly by lot and found hidden among the stuff. Is Saul also among the prophets?
chapters.11: Jabesh-gilead threatened with the loss of every right eye. Saul hews a yoke of oxen in pieces and the nation musters.
chapters.12: Samuel's farewell, with thunder and rain in wheat harvest as a sign. God forbid that I should sin in ceasing to pray for you.
chapters.13: Saul sacrifices rather than wait seven days for Samuel. The kingdom will not continue. No smith was found in all Israel.
chapters.14: Jonathan and his armourbearer climb up alone and start a rout. Saul's rash oath, and honey on the ground the army may not eat.
chapters.15: Amalek spared in part. To obey is better than sacrifice — and Samuel hews Agag in pieces and does not see Saul again.
chapters.16: Samuel sent to Jesse: man looketh on the outward appearance. David anointed, and later brought in to play the harp for Saul.
chapters.17: Goliath's height, armour and daily challenge. Five smooth stones, and the refusal of Saul's armour because he had not proved it.
chapters.18: Jonathan's soul knit with David's. The women's song about thousands and ten thousands, and the javelin thrown twice.
chapters.19: Michal lets David down through a window and puts an image in the bed. Saul pursues to Naioth and ends up prophesying himself.
chapters.20: The new moon feast, the covenant between David and Jonathan, and the arrows shot beyond the lad as a signal.
chapters.21: David eats the shewbread at Nob and takes Goliath's sword. In Gath he escapes by feigning madness and scrabbling on the gate.
chapters.22: The cave of Adullam gathers everyone in distress or debt. Doeg the Edomite kills eighty-five priests; Abiathar alone escapes.
chapters.23: David saves Keilah and is nearly betrayed by it. The Ziphites report him, and Jonathan comes to strengthen his hand in God.
chapters.24: In the cave at Engedi David cuts off Saul's skirt and his heart smites him for it. Saul weeps and admits David will be king.
chapters.25: Nabal's insult and Abigail's swift diplomacy with loaves, raisins and figs. Nabal's heart dies within him ten days later.
chapters.26: David takes the spear and cruse of water from beside Saul's head as he sleeps in the trench, and calls across the valley.
chapters.27: David defects to Achish of Gath and is given Ziklag, raiding elsewhere while reporting otherwise.
chapters.28: Saul, with Samuel dead and God silent, seeks a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor, having himself put such people out of the land.
chapters.29: The Philistine lords refuse to let David fight beside them, which spares him from the battle that kills Saul.
chapters.30: Ziklag burned and the families taken. David pursues, and rules that those who stayed with the stuff share the spoil alike.
chapters.31: Gilboa. Saul falls on his own sword; the men of Jabesh-gilead take the bodies down from the wall by night and burn them.

books.name: 2 Samuel
books.scribe: Nathan and Gad, the court prophets, per 1 Chr 29:29.
rulers: DAVID (c. 1010–970) — 7 years in Hebron, 33 in Jerusalem
books.summary: David unites the tribes, takes Jerusalem, and receives a covenant of an everlasting throne — then commits adultery and murder, and spends the rest of the book living in the wreckage.
prophecies: 2 Sam 7:12–16 — the Davidic covenant: I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Seven years over Judah in Hebron, then all Israel; Jerusalem taken.
The ark brought up, the covenant of an everlasting throne, victories.
Adultery, murder, Nathan's parable, a child dies.
Rape, fratricide, Absalom's coup, David fleeing barefoot.
Famine, giants, David's psalm, and a census that costs 70,000 lives.

chapters.1: The Amalekite who claims to have killed Saul is executed for it. Then the lament: how are the mighty fallen.
chapters.2: David anointed over Judah at Hebron while Abner sets up Ish-bosheth. The contest at the pool of Gibeon and the death of Asahel.
chapters.3: Abner defects and is murdered by Joab in the gate. David refuses to eat and follows the bier.
chapters.4: Ish-bosheth murdered in his bed by two captains, who bring the head to David expecting reward and are executed instead.
chapters.5: David king over all Israel at thirty-seven. Jerusalem taken from the Jebusites by the gutter, and named the city of David.
chapters.6: The ark on a new cart. Uzzah steadies it and dies; three months later it comes up properly, with David dancing and Michal despising him.
chapters.7: David wants to build a house and is told instead that God will build him one. The covenant with David, echoing through the rest of scripture.
chapters.8: A summary of the wars — Philistines, Moab, Zobah, Syria, Edom — and the officers of the kingdom.
chapters.9: Is there yet any that is left of the house of Saul? Mephibosheth, lame on both feet, eats at the king's table continually.
chapters.10: Ambassadors humiliated by Hanun of Ammon, their beards half shaved. The Syrian coalition defeated.
chapters.11: The year when kings go forth to battle, and David stayed at Jerusalem. Bathsheba, then Uriah, then the letter Uriah carries himself.
chapters.12: Nathan's parable of the ewe lamb, and thou art the man. The child dies; Solomon is born and called Jedidiah.
chapters.13: Amnon and Tamar, and Absalom's two years of silence before the sheepshearing at Baal-hazor.
chapters.14: Joab sends the woman of Tekoah with a made-up case. Absalom is brought back but not seen, until he sets Joab's barley on fire.
chapters.15: Absalom steals the hearts of the men of Israel at the gate. David leaves Jerusalem barefoot and weeping up Olivet.
chapters.16: Ziba's convenient story about Mephibosheth, and Shimei cursing and throwing stones, whom David will not let anyone silence.
chapters.17: Ahithophel's sound advice defeated by Hushai's flattering alternative. Ahithophel goes home, sets his house in order, and hangs himself.
chapters.18: Absalom caught by his head in an oak. Joab kills him against orders, and David's cry: O my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee.
chapters.19: The return, with Judah and Israel quarrelling over who owns the king. Shimei pardoned; Barzillai too old to come.
chapters.20: Sheba's revolt, ended by a wise woman of Abel throwing his head over the wall.
chapters.21: Three years of famine traced to Saul's slaughter of the Gibeonites. Rizpah watching the bodies from harvest until the rain.
chapters.22: David's song of deliverance, almost identical to Psalm 18.
chapters.23: The last words of David, then the roll of the mighty men — and the three who broke through the Philistines for water he would not drink.
chapters.24: The census and the plague. David buys the threshingfloor of Araunah, refusing to offer that which costs him nothing.

books.name: 1 Kings
books.full: The First Book of the Kings
books.scribe: Compiled by an unnamed scribe — Jewish tradition says Jeremiah — from court records: 'the book of the acts of Solomon' and the chronicles of both kingdoms are cited by name.
rulers: Rehoboam and Jeroboam I — the split
books.summary: Solomon builds the Temple and loses his heart to foreign wives. At his death ten tribes walk out, and the book follows two kingdoms downhill until Elijah faces Ahab on Carmel.
prophecies: 1 Kgs 11:11–13 — I will rend the kingdom from thee
1 Kgs 13:2 — a child named Josiah, three centuries before his birth
books.power: Egypt raids under Shishak; Syria pressures the north
books.captivity: None yet — tribute and vassalage begin.

moves.n: Wisdom asked for, the Temple built, the queen of Sheba, then the foreign wives.
Rehoboam's ultimatum, ten tribes gone, two lines of kings begin.
Drought, ravens, Carmel, the still small voice, Naboth's vineyard.

chapters.1: Adonijah proclaims himself king while David is old and cold. Nathan and Bathsheba move fast; Solomon is anointed at Gihon.
chapters.2: David's last charge, including old scores. Solomon settles with Adonijah, Joab at the altar, Abiathar and Shimei.
chapters.3: At Gibeon Solomon asks for an understanding heart. Then the two women and the living child divided by the sword — or not.
chapters.4: The administration listed, and the reach of the wisdom: three thousand proverbs, and trees from cedar to hyssop.
chapters.5: The agreement with Hiram of Tyre: cedar and fir floated down in flotes, paid for in wheat and oil.
chapters.6: The temple built in seven years, in the four hundred and eightieth year after the exodus. No hammer or axe heard in the house.
chapters.7: Solomon's own house takes thirteen years. Hiram the bronzeworker makes the two pillars, the molten sea on twelve oxen, and the lavers.
chapters.8: The ark brought in, the cloud filling the house, and Solomon's long dedication prayer — will God indeed dwell on the earth?
chapters.9: The LORD appears a second time with a warning attached. Cities given to Hiram which displease him, and the navy at Ezion-geber.
chapters.10: The queen of Sheba comes to prove him with hard questions and finds the half was not told her. Six hundred threescore and six talents of gold.
chapters.11: Foreign wives turn his heart. Adversaries raised up, and Ahijah tears a new garment into twelve pieces for Jeroboam.
chapters.12: Rehoboam takes the young men's counsel about scorpions. Ten tribes secede; Jeroboam makes two calves, at Bethel and Dan.
chapters.13: The man of God from Judah who cries against the altar, is deceived by an old prophet, and is killed by a lion that does not eat him.
chapters.14: Jeroboam's wife disguised and recognised by a blind prophet. Shishak of Egypt carries off the treasures; brasen shields replace gold.
chapters.15: Abijam and Asa in Judah, Nadab and Baasha in Israel. Asa removes his own mother from being queen.
chapters.16: Four kings in quick succession, Zimri's seven days, and then Omri and Ahab, who did evil above all that were before him.
chapters.17: Elijah announces the drought and is fed by ravens, then by a widow of Zarephath whose barrel of meal does not waste.
chapters.18: Carmel. Cry aloud, for he is a god. The fire falls, and then a cloud the size of a man's hand.
chapters.19: Under a juniper tree he asks to die. Fed by an angel, he goes to Horeb: wind, earthquake, fire, and then a still small voice.
chapters.20: Ben-hadad besieges Samaria twice and is defeated twice. Ahab lets him go and a prophet in disguise condemns him for it.
chapters.21: Naboth will not sell his vineyard. Jezebel arranges a fast, false witnesses and a stoning; Elijah meets Ahab in the vineyard itself.
chapters.22: Four hundred prophets say go up. Micaiah, fetched reluctantly, says otherwise. Ahab is killed by an arrow shot at a venture.

books.name: 2 Kings
books.full: The Second Book of the Kings
books.scribe: Same compiler as 1 Kings; traditionally Jeremiah, writing during or just after the exile.
books.summary: Both kingdoms run out of time. Samaria falls to Assyria in 722 and the ten tribes vanish into Media; Judah lasts to 586, when Jerusalem is burned and the people carried to Babylon.
themes: The word of the LORD coming true
prophecies: 2 Kgs 20:17–18 — Isaiah tells Hezekiah all shall be carried to Babylon, a century early
2 Kgs 22:16–20 — Huldah's prophecy that Josiah will not see the disaster
books.captivity: BOTH. The northern deportation in 722, the southern in 605/597/586.

moves.n: Elijah taken up; a double portion; healings, sieges and floating iron.
Jehu's purge, decline, and Samaria taken by Assyria in 722.
Hezekiah's deliverance, Manasseh's evil, Josiah's reform, Babylon.

chapters.1: Ahaziah falls through a lattice and sends to Baal-zebub. Two companies of fifty are consumed; the third captain asks rather than commands.
chapters.2: Elijah taken up by a whirlwind with a chariot of fire. Elisha takes the mantle, and the children of Bethel and the two she bears.
chapters.3: The campaign against Moab through a waterless wilderness. Ditches filled without wind or rain, and water that looks red as blood.
chapters.4: The widow's pot of oil, the Shunammite's son raised, death in the pot cured with meal, and a hundred men fed with twenty loaves.
chapters.5: Naaman's leprosy, the little maid, and his anger at being told to wash in Jordan seven times. Gehazi takes the payment and the disease.
chapters.6: The axe head that swims, an army struck blind and led to Samaria, then a siege so bad that women eat their children.
chapters.7: Four lepers at the gate find the Syrian camp abandoned. Why sit we here until we die? The lord who doubted is trodden down in the gate.
chapters.8: The Shunammite's land restored. Hazael smothers Ben-hadad with a wet cloth and takes the throne, as Elisha wept foreseeing.
chapters.9: Jehu anointed and driving furiously. Joram shot through the heart; Jezebel thrown from a window and eaten by dogs.
chapters.10: Seventy heads in baskets, and the worshippers of Baal gathered into their own house and killed. Jehu does not depart from the calves.
chapters.11: Athaliah destroys the seed royal, but Joash is hidden six years in the temple. The crowning, and Athaliah crying Treason.
chapters.12: Joash orders the temple repaired, and a chest with a hole in the lid is set beside the altar when the priests are slow.
chapters.13: Jehoahaz and Joash of Israel. Elisha dying tells the king to smite the ground, and is angry that he stops at three.
chapters.14: Amaziah picks a fight with Israel using a parable about a thistle and a cedar, and loses. Jeroboam II restores the borders.
chapters.15: Five kings of Israel in one chapter, four of them assassinated. Pul of Assyria appears, and the money to buy him off.
chapters.16: Ahaz hires Assyria against Syria and copies a Damascus altar for the temple, moving the brasen altar aside.
chapters.17: Samaria falls after three years. A long explanation of why, then the resettlement that produces the Samaritans of the Gospels.
chapters.18: Hezekiah's reform, including breaking the brasen serpent. Sennacherib's invasion, and Rabshakeh's speech in the Jews' language on the wall.
chapters.19: Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD. Isaiah answers, and the angel of the LORD smites the camp in the night.
chapters.20: Hezekiah's illness, the fig poultice, and the shadow going backward ten degrees. Then he shows the Babylonian envoys everything.
chapters.21: Manasseh, fifty-five years and the worst of them — altars in the house, his son passed through the fire, innocent blood filling Jerusalem.
chapters.22: The book of the law found during repairs. Josiah rends his clothes, and Huldah the prophetess is consulted.
chapters.23: The reform: high places defiled, the Asherah burned, mediums put away, and a passover such as had not been kept since the judges. Josiah dies at Megiddo.
chapters.24: Jehoiakim, then Jehoiachin who reigns three months and is carried to Babylon with ten thousand captives and all the craftsmen.
chapters.25: The siege, the breach, the burning of the house. Zedekiah blinded, Gedaliah murdered — and at the very end, Jehoiachin brought out of prison and given a seat.

books.name: 1 Chronicles
books.full: The First Book of the Chronicles
books.scribe: Ezra, by long tradition — a priest-scribe writing for the returned exiles. Nine chapters of genealogy show a people re-establishing who they are.
books.written: c. 450–430 BC, about events up to 970
rulers: David, retold for a people with no king
books.summary: The same history as Samuel and Kings, retold after the exile for people rebuilding. It skips the northern kingdom entirely and concentrates on David, the ark, and the plans for the Temple.
prophecies: 1 Chr 17:11–14 — the Davidic covenant restated to a nation without a throne
books.captivity: Returned, but a province.

moves.n: Nine chapters tracing Adam to the returning exiles.
Saul's death, the mighty men listed by name.
Uzzah, the tent, and the promise of an everlasting house.
Materials, Levites, singers, gatekeepers — and the handover to Solomon.

chapters.1: Nine chapters of genealogy open the book. This one runs from Adam to Esau, compressing the whole of Genesis into lists of names.
chapters.2: The sons of Israel, then Judah traced in detail down to the house of Jesse — the line the Chronicler cares about most.
chapters.3: The sons of David, then the kings of Judah in order, carried past the exile to Zerubbabel's descendants.
chapters.4: More of Judah and Simeon, interrupted by the prayer of Jabez, who asked that God would enlarge his coast.
chapters.5: Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh east of Jordan, with a note that they were carried away for trusting in their own numbers.
chapters.6: Levi at length: the high priestly line, the singers David set over the service of song, and the Levitical cities.
chapters.7: Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim and Asher, mostly as muster rolls of fighting men.
chapters.8: Benjamin again in more detail, ending with the house of Saul — placed here to set up the next chapter.
chapters.9: Those who returned and lived in Jerusalem, with the porters and their duties, then Saul's genealogy repeated.
chapters.10: Saul's death on Gilboa, told in a single chapter, with the Chronicler's verdict: he died for his transgression.
chapters.11: David made king at Hebron and Jerusalem taken. The roll of the mighty men, and the three who broke through for water.
chapters.12: Those who came to David at Ziklag, including the men of Issachar who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do.
chapters.13: The ark on a cart. Uzza puts out his hand and dies, and David is afraid to bring it further.
chapters.14: David's house built, his family listed, and two victories over the Philistines after enquiring both times.
chapters.15: The ark carried properly this time, on the shoulders of the Levites, with singers and instruments appointed.
chapters.16: Asaph's psalm of thanksgiving, assembled from Psalms 105, 96 and 106. O give thanks unto the LORD; call upon his name.
chapters.17: Nathan's oracle: David will not build the house, but God will build him one. David's answer — who am I, O LORD God?
chapters.18: A summary of the wars, from Moab to the Euphrates, and the officers who served him.
chapters.19: The Ammonite insult to David's envoys and the war that follows, with Joab and Abishai dividing the field.
chapters.20: Rabbah taken, and three encounters with giants — the Chronicler passes over the Bathsheba affair entirely.
chapters.21: The census, Joab's protest, and the plague stopped at the threshingfloor of Ornan, bought for six hundred shekels of gold.
chapters.22: David gathers iron, brass and cedar beyond weight, and charges Solomon: be strong, and of good courage, and do it.
chapters.23: The Levites numbered from thirty years old and upward, and their work redefined now that the tabernacle no longer needs carrying.
chapters.24: The twenty-four courses of priests settled by lot — the arrangement Zacharias is serving under in Luke 1.
chapters.25: The singers set apart, to prophesy with harps, psalteries and cymbals, also divided by lot into twenty-four courses.
chapters.26: The porters assigned gate by gate, and the treasurers over the dedicated things won in battle.
chapters.27: The twelve monthly courses of the army, the princes of the tribes, and the officers over David's fields, herds and cellars.
chapters.28: David's charge before the whole assembly, and the pattern of the temple given in writing, which he says came from the hand of the LORD.
chapters.29: The offerings given willingly, and David's prayer: all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee. Solomon anointed; David dies full of days.

books.name: 2 Chronicles
books.full: The Second Book of the Chronicles
books.scribe: Ezra, by tradition. Cites the records of Nathan, Ahijah, Iddo, Shemaiah and Jehu son of Hanani as sources.
rulers: Cyrus, whose decree ends the book
books.summary: Solomon's Temple to its burning, told through Judah's kings and their reforms. It closes mid-sentence with Cyrus telling the exiles to go home and build.
prophecies: 2 Chr 7:14 — if my people shall humble themselves… then will I heal their land
2 Chr 36:21 — the land kept sabbath seventy years, fulfilling Jeremiah
laws: Sabbath years owed and repaid through exile (36:21)
books.captivity: Ends with the decree of release.

moves.n: Wisdom, Temple, dedication, wealth, Sheba.
Rehoboam through Jehoshaphat, with Judah alone in view.
Athaliah's coup, Joash, Uzziah's leprosy, Ahaz's idolatry.
Hezekiah and Josiah's revivals; then Babylon, and Cyrus.

chapters.1: Solomon at Gibeon asks for wisdom and knowledge rather than riches, and is given all three.
chapters.2: The letter to Huram of Tyre, and the levy of workmen. The house must be great, for great is our God above all gods.
chapters.3: The temple begun in mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David, on the threshingfloor of Ornan.
chapters.4: The furnishings: the molten sea on twelve oxen, ten lavers, ten candlesticks, and the vessels beyond weight.
chapters.5: The ark brought in. The singers and trumpeters make one sound, and the cloud fills the house so the priests cannot stand to minister.
chapters.6: Solomon's prayer of dedication from a brasen scaffold — seven petitions, each asking that God hear from heaven and forgive.
chapters.7: Fire comes down and consumes the offering. Then the night answer: if my people shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face.
chapters.8: Building projects, the cities of store, and the observance that Pharaoh's daughter should not live in David's house because the places are holy.
chapters.9: The queen of Sheba's visit, the ivory throne with twelve lions, and Solomon's death after forty years.
chapters.10: Rehoboam at Shechem, the old men's counsel refused, and the kingdom torn in two.
chapters.11: Rehoboam fortifies Judah, and the priests and Levites come over to him from all Israel because Jeroboam cast them off.
chapters.12: When he was strong, he forsook the law. Shishak takes the treasures; the shields of gold are replaced with brass.
chapters.13: Abijah's speech from mount Zemaraim before the battle, and a victory attributed to relying upon the LORD.
chapters.14: Asa's reform and the invasion of Zerah the Ethiopian with a thousand thousand men, met with a prayer.
chapters.15: Azariah's word: the LORD is with you, while ye be with him. Asa renews the covenant and removes his own grandmother's idol.
chapters.16: Asa hires Syria against Israel and is rebuked for it. Diseased in his feet, he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians.
chapters.17: Jehoshaphat sends princes, Levites and priests through the cities of Judah with the book of the law to teach.
chapters.18: The alliance with Ahab by marriage, and the Micaiah episode retold almost word for word from 1 Kings 22.
chapters.19: Rebuked for helping the ungodly, Jehoshaphat sets judges in the land: take heed what ye do, for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD.
chapters.20: A vast invasion met by fasting and a prayer ending we know not what to do, but our eyes are upon thee. The singers go out ahead of the army.
chapters.21: Jehoram kills his brothers, and receives a writing from Elijah. He departs without being desired.
chapters.22: Ahaziah's one year, then Athaliah destroying the seed royal, and Joash hidden in the house of God.
chapters.23: Jehoiada's carefully staged coup, with the Levites armed from David's own store and the boy king crowned in the temple.
chapters.24: Joash repairs the house while Jehoiada lives, then turns after his death and has Zechariah stoned in the court.
chapters.25: Amaziah hires Israelite mercenaries, sends them home at a prophet's word, then worships the gods of the people he has just defeated.
chapters.26: Uzziah prospers while he seeks God, then burns incense in the temple himself and is a leper to the day of his death.
chapters.27: Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God. One short chapter, and no failure recorded.
chapters.28: Ahaz at his worst — and the striking episode where the prophet Oded persuades Israel to clothe and feed their Judean captives and send them home.
chapters.29: Hezekiah opens the doors of the house in the first month of his reign and has sixteen days of cleaning done before worship resumes.
chapters.30: A passover kept in the second month because the priests were not ready, with invitations sent to what was left of the northern tribes.
chapters.31: Tithes heaped in piles, chambers prepared, and the portions of the priests and Levites restored so they could attend to the law.
chapters.32: Sennacherib's invasion, the conduit brought into the city, Hezekiah's illness and the pride of heart that followed.
chapters.33: Manasseh carried to Babylon with hooks, and there humbling himself — a repentance 2 Kings does not record. Then Amon.
chapters.34: Josiah begins seeking God at sixteen and purging at twenty. The book of the law found during the repairs.
chapters.35: A passover unequalled since Samuel, with the Levites organised in courses. Then Megiddo, and Jeremiah's lament for him.
chapters.36: Four kings in as many paragraphs, the burning of the house, seventy years for the land to enjoy her sabbaths, and Cyrus's decree — the last words of the Hebrew Bible.

books.name: Ezra
books.scribe: Ezra the priest and scribe. Chapters 7–10 shift into first person — he is writing about himself.
books.summary: Two returns, eighty years apart. The first rebuilds the altar and the Temple against local opposition; the second brings Ezra with the Law and a hard reform of intermarriage.
prophecies: Ezra 1:1 — the decree of Cyrus, expressly to fulfil the word by Jeremiah
laws: Ezra teaches and enforces the law of Moses in the province (7:10, 25–26)
books.captivity: CAPTIVITY ENDED — 539 BC, by decree.

moves.n: Cyrus's decree, Zerubbabel's caravan, altar and foundation, opposition, temple finished.
Eighty years later: a scribe, a commission, and a painful reform.

chapters.1: Cyrus makes a proclamation in the first year of his reign. The vessels Nebuchadnezzar took are counted back out by name.
chapters.2: The register of those who went up, family by family, down to the singers, the porters and the horses. Some cannot prove their genealogy.
chapters.3: The altar set up first, before a stone of the temple is laid. At the foundation the old men who had seen the first house weep aloud.
chapters.4: Offers of help refused, so the neighbours hire counsellors and write to the king. The work stops until the reign of Darius.
chapters.5: Haggai and Zechariah start them building again. Tattenai the governor asks who commanded this, and writes to Darius.
chapters.6: The original decree found at Achmetha. Darius orders the work paid for out of his own tribute; the house is finished and dedicated.
chapters.7: Ezra comes up nearly sixty years later, a ready scribe in the law of Moses, with a remarkable letter of authority from Artaxerxes.
chapters.8: The heads of families listed. A fast at the river Ahava, because Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers after boasting of God's protection.
chapters.9: The report of intermarriage. Ezra tears his garment, plucks off his hair, and sits astonied until the evening sacrifice.
chapters.10: The assembly in the rain, and the painful separation that follows, with the names of those involved set down.

books.name: Nehemiah
books.scribe: Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes — written as a first-person memoir, possibly edited into place by Ezra.
books.summary: A wall goes up in fifty-two days under armed guard. Then the harder work: reading the Law aloud, confessing, and holding a covenant together against debt, mixed marriage and Sabbath trade.
laws: Debt relief and the return of pledged fields (5)
Sabbath trade shut down at the gates (13:15–22)
books.captivity: Free, walled, still taxed by Persia.

moves.n: Nehemiah's prayer, the king's leave, the night ride, fifty-two days of building under threat.
Ezra reads aloud from morning to midday; the people weep, then covenant.
The city repopulated, dedicated — and abuses returning by the last chapter.

chapters.1: News reaches Susa that the wall is broken down and the gates burned. Nehemiah weeps, fasts and prays for days.
chapters.2: The king notices his sadness. Nehemiah asks for timber and letters, then rides round the ruins by night telling no one.
chapters.3: The builders listed gate by gate — goldsmiths, apothecaries, rulers, and the daughters of Shallum. The nobles of Tekoa would not stoop to it.
chapters.4: Sanballat's mockery about a fox breaking down the stone wall. Every builder works with one hand and holds a weapon with the other.
chapters.5: An internal crisis: Jews mortgaging children to Jews. Nehemiah shakes out his lap and gives up his own governor's allowance.
chapters.6: Four invitations to meet in the plain of Ono, a false letter, and a hired prophet. The wall is finished in fifty-two days.
chapters.7: The gates guarded, and the register of chapter 2 in Ezra repeated as the basis for repopulating the city.
chapters.8: Ezra reads the law from morning until midday, standing on a pulpit of wood, with Levites giving the sense. The joy of the LORD is your strength.
chapters.9: A day of confession retelling the whole history, from Abraham through the wilderness, with the refrain that God is ready to pardon.
chapters.10: The sealed covenant, with signatories named and specific undertakings about marriage, sabbath, debts and the temple.
chapters.11: Lots cast to bring one in ten to live in Jerusalem, and the people bless everyone who willingly offered themselves.
chapters.12: The dedication of the wall, with two great companies of singers going opposite ways along the top and meeting at the house of God.
chapters.13: Nehemiah returns after an absence and finds Tobiah in a temple chamber, tithes unpaid, wine presses working on the sabbath, and mixed marriages. He deals with all four bluntly.

books.name: Esther
books.scribe: Unknown — written by someone with detailed knowledge of the Persian court. Mordecai is the traditional candidate.
rulers: Xerxes I, the Ahasuerus of the book (486–465 BC)
books.summary: The Jews who did not go home come within a decree of extermination. God is never named in the book, and the rescue happens entirely through timing, courage and a king's insomnia.
laws: The feast of Purim established as binding on the Jews and their seed (9:27–28)
books.captivity: Diaspora — free to leave, choosing to stay.

moves.n: Vashti refuses, and a search brings Esther to the palace.
Haman's decree, Mordecai's grief, Esther's fast and first banquet.
The king cannot sleep, reads the chronicles, and Haman's day inverts.
A counter-decree, the Jews defend themselves, Purim established.

chapters.1: A feast of a hundred and eighty days. Vashti refuses to be displayed and is deposed, on the advice that all wives will hear of it.
chapters.2: The search for a new queen. Esther does not shew her people. Mordecai uncovers a plot and it is written in the chronicles.
chapters.3: Haman promoted and enraged by one man who will not bow. Lots cast for the day, and a decree to destroy all Jews in one day.
chapters.4: Sackcloth in the gate. Mordecai's message: who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this. If I perish, I perish.
chapters.5: The golden sceptre held out. Esther invites the king and Haman to a banquet, then to a second. Haman builds a gallows fifty cubits high.
chapters.6: The king cannot sleep, has the chronicles read, and asks Haman what should be done for the man the king delights to honour.
chapters.7: At the second banquet Esther names him. The king walks out to the garden; Haman falls on the couch, and is hanged on his own gallows.
chapters.8: A decree cannot be revoked, so a second is written allowing the Jews to defend themselves, sent by posts on swift camels.
chapters.9: The thirteenth day turns. The ten sons of Haman are hanged, and the feast of Purim is established with letters to every province.
chapters.10: Three verses on the greatness of Mordecai, seeking the wealth of his people and speaking peace to all his seed.

books.name: Job
books.scribe: Unknown, and possibly the oldest book in the Bible — the setting is patriarchal, with wealth counted in livestock and no mention of Israel, the Law or the Temple.
books.written: Setting c. 2000–1800 BC; written down far later
rulers: No king — Job is a clan head in the land of Uz
