books.summary: A blameless man loses everything, and three friends spend thirty chapters explaining why he must deserve it. God finally answers, and never explains — he asks questions instead.
themes: God's answer as presence, not argument
prophecies: Job 19:25 — I know that my redeemer liveth
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Job loses property, children and health in two days.
Three friends in three rounds; Job answers every one.
A younger man who has been listening the whole time.
Out of the whirlwind, in questions — and Job's restoration.

chapters.1: A prose prologue. Job is blameless and rich; the accuser asks whether he serves God for nothing. Four messengers arrive, each before the last has finished.
chapters.2: A second wager, and boils from sole to crown. His wife tells him to curse God and die. Three friends sit seven days without a word.
chapters.3: Job breaks the silence by cursing the day of his birth. Let that day be darkness. He does not curse God, which is the point.
chapters.4: Eliphaz begins gently, then describes a spirit passing before his face and the hair of his flesh standing up.
chapters.5: Man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward. Eliphaz counsels seeking unto God, and promises restoration.
chapters.6: Job answers that his grief would outweigh the sand of the sea. His friends are like a brook that dries up when travellers need it.
chapters.7: My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle. He asks to be let alone until he swallow down his spittle.
chapters.8: Bildad appeals to tradition: enquire of the former age. Can the rush grow up without mire?
chapters.9: How should man be just with God? Job wants a court but there is no daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both.
chapters.10: I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. Thine hands have made me, and yet thou dost destroy me.
chapters.11: Zophar, the bluntest of the three: canst thou by searching find out God? He assumes Job is hiding something.
chapters.12: Ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee. Job matches their proverbs with his own and says he is not inferior.
chapters.13: Ye are all physicians of no value. Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him — but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
chapters.14: Man that is born of a woman is of few days. A tree cut down may sprout again; he asks whether a man does.
chapters.15: Eliphaz's second speech, harder than his first: thine own mouth condemneth thee.
chapters.16: Miserable comforters are ye all. Yet Job appeals past them: my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high.
chapters.17: The grave is mine house; I have made my bed in the darkness. He asks who will strike hands with him as surety.
chapters.18: Bildad describes the fate of the wicked at length, all of it aimed at Job by implication.
chapters.19: He has been abandoned by everyone, down to his own servants. Then: I know that my redeemer liveth, and yet in my flesh shall I see God.
chapters.20: Zophar: the triumphing of the wicked is short. He swallows down riches and vomits them up again.
chapters.21: Job's decisive counter-argument: wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power? Experience contradicts the theory.
chapters.22: Eliphaz abandons hints and invents charges — you stripped the naked of their clothing, you sent widows away empty.
chapters.23: Oh that I knew where I might find him. He would order his cause before him, and he trusts he would come forth as gold.
chapters.24: A catalogue of injustice that goes unpunished: landmarks removed, the poor gleaning in another man's field.
chapters.25: Bildad's third speech is six verses and then nothing. The friends have run out of arguments.
chapters.26: Job answers with a hymn to power: he stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing.
chapters.27: Till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me. He will not concede a case he knows is false.
chapters.28: A poem on wisdom set apart from everything around it. Miners find silver and sapphires in the dark, but where shall wisdom be found?
chapters.29: Job remembers the days when the young men saw him and hid, and he was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.
chapters.30: But now they that are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I would have disdained to set with the dogs of my flock.
chapters.31: A long oath of innocence, clause by clause — eyes, servants, the poor, the stranger, even his land. The words of Job are ended.
chapters.32: Elihu, who has been listening all along, is angry with everyone. He is young and says so at length before saying anything else.
chapters.33: Elihu's argument: God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not. Suffering may be instruction rather than punishment.
chapters.34: Far be it from God, that he should do wickedness. Elihu defends divine justice in the abstract.
chapters.35: If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? Elihu argues that human conduct does not injure God.
chapters.36: Behold, God is great, and we know him not. Elihu begins turning toward the weather.
chapters.37: The storm arrives while he is still speaking — the thunder, the frost, the balancings of the clouds.
chapters.38: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind. Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? Question after question, none of them Job's.
chapters.39: Wild goats, the wild ass, the ostrich who leaveth her eggs in the earth, the horse who saith among the trumpets Ha, ha.
chapters.40: Job puts his hand upon his mouth. Then behemoth, who moveth his tail like a cedar.
chapters.41: Leviathan, described for a whole chapter, whom none is so fierce that dare stir up.
chapters.42: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee. The friends are rebuked and Job prays for them.

books.name: Psalms
books.scribe: A collection by many hands over ~1,000 years: 73 attributed to David, 12 to Asaph, 11 to the sons of Korah, 2 to Solomon, one to Moses (Ps 90), and about 50 anonymous. Arranged into five books.
rulers: the exiles by the rivers of Babylon
books.summary: Israel's hymnbook and prayer book, covering the whole range from praise to rage. Five books, each closing with a doxology, mirroring the five books of Moses.
prophecies: Ps 2 — thou art my Son
Ps 22 — they pierced my hands and my feet
Ps 110 — a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek
laws: Ps 19 and Ps 119 — extended meditations on the law itself
books.captivity: Ps 137 is written in Babylon.

moves.n: Mostly David. Opens with the two ways and closes with a doxology.
Korah and David; ends with the note that David's prayers are ended.
Asaph's psalms; the darkest section, wrestling with national collapse.
Opens with Moses' psalm; the LORD reigns over the nations.
Songs of degrees, the great acrostic 119, and five closing hallelujahs.

chapters.1: The gate of the whole book: two ways set side by side. The tree planted by rivers of water against chaff the wind drives away.
chapters.2: Why do the heathen rage. A coronation psalm — thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee — quoted repeatedly in the New Testament.
chapters.3: A morning psalm of David fleeing Absalom. I laid me down and slept; I awaked, for the LORD sustained me.
chapters.4: An evening companion to Psalm 3. Stand in awe, and sin not; commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still.
chapters.5: A morning prayer at the time of sacrifice. My voice shalt thou hear in the morning; I will direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
chapters.6: The first of the seven penitential psalms. I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim.
chapters.7: A plea for vindication against slander, with the image of the wicked digging a pit and falling into it himself.
chapters.8: What is man, that thou art mindful of him? Set between the heavens as the work of his fingers and the beasts under his feet.
chapters.9: Thanksgiving for judgment on the nations. An acrostic that continues into Psalm 10, which is why Psalm 10 lacks a title.
chapters.10: Why standest thou afar off? The wicked described in detail — he hath said in his heart, God hath forgotten.
chapters.11: If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do? The answer is that the LORD is in his holy temple.
chapters.12: The words of the LORD are pure words, as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.
chapters.13: How long? asked four times in two verses, then resolved in three: but I have trusted in thy mercy.
chapters.14: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Repeated almost word for word as Psalm 53, and quoted in Romans 3.
chapters.15: Who shall abide in thy tabernacle? A short list of conduct: walks uprightly, speaks truth, sweareth to his own hurt and changeth not.
chapters.16: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell. Quoted by Peter at Pentecost. In thy presence is fulness of joy.
chapters.17: Keep me as the apple of the eye; hide me under the shadow of thy wings.
chapters.18: A long royal thanksgiving after deliverance from Saul, with God descending on a cherub and riding on the wings of the wind. Repeated in 2 Samuel 22.
chapters.19: The heavens declare the glory of God — then the law of the LORD is perfect. Two witnesses, sky and scripture, in one psalm.
chapters.20: A prayer before battle. Some trust in chariots, and some in horses; but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
chapters.21: The answer to Psalm 20, celebrating the king's victory and the length of days given him.
chapters.22: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me. They pierced my hands and my feet; they part my garments. Quoted from the cross.
chapters.23: The LORD is my shepherd. Green pastures, still waters, the valley of the shadow, and a table prepared in the presence of enemies.
chapters.24: Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? Then the gates lifting up their heads for the King of glory to come in.
chapters.25: An acrostic prayer for guidance and pardon. Remember not the sins of my youth.
chapters.26: A protest of integrity. I have walked in mine integrity; examine me, O LORD, and prove me.
chapters.27: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? One thing have I desired — to dwell in the house of the LORD.
chapters.28: A cry not to be silent, answered mid-psalm: blessed be the LORD, because he hath heard the voice of my supplications.
chapters.29: The voice of the LORD sounded seven times over the waters, breaking the cedars of Lebanon. A thunderstorm psalm.
chapters.30: At the dedication of the house. Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
chapters.31: Into thine hand I commit my spirit — the words Jesus speaks last from the cross.
chapters.32: Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven. The bones waxing old through silence, and the release of confession. Quoted in Romans 4.
chapters.33: Praise with the harp and an instrument of ten strings. By the word of the LORD were the heavens made.
chapters.34: An acrostic written after David feigned madness before Abimelech. O taste and see that the LORD is good.
chapters.35: A cry against those who reward evil for good, and who hated me without a cause.
chapters.36: The wicked flattering himself in his own eyes, set against mercy reaching to the heavens and the fountain of life.
chapters.37: Fret not thyself because of evildoers. An acrostic on the shortness of the wicked's prosperity, and the meek inheriting the earth.
chapters.38: A penitential psalm of sickness and abandonment. There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger.
chapters.39: Lord, make me to know mine end. Man walketh in a vain shew; he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them.
chapters.40: He brought me up out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay. Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened.
chapters.41: Blessed is he that considereth the poor. Mine own familiar friend hath lifted up his heel against me — quoted at the last supper.
chapters.42: Book Two opens. As the hart panteth after the water brooks. Why art thou cast down, O my soul? asked three times across two psalms.
chapters.43: The completion of Psalm 42, sharing its refrain. Send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me.
chapters.44: A national lament for a defeat that was not deserved. We are counted as sheep for the slaughter — quoted in Romans 8.
chapters.45: A royal wedding song, addressed to the king and then to the bride. Quoted in Hebrews 1 as addressed to the Son.
chapters.46: God is our refuge and strength. Though the earth be removed, and the mountains carried into the sea. Be still, and know that I am God.
chapters.47: God is gone up with a shout. An enthronement psalm calling all people to clap their hands.
chapters.48: Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth, is mount Zion. Walk about her and tell the towers thereof.
chapters.49: A wisdom psalm on the futility of wealth: none can redeem his brother, and they carry nothing away when they die.
chapters.50: God speaks and asks what sacrifice is for. If I were hungry, I would not tell thee, for the cattle upon a thousand hills are mine.
chapters.51: David's psalm after Nathan came to him. Create in me a clean heart; the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.
chapters.52: Against Doeg the Edomite, who informed on the priests at Nob. Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man?
chapters.53: A second version of Psalm 14, with slight variations and the divine name changed throughout.
chapters.54: A short prayer written when the Ziphims betrayed David's hiding place to Saul.
chapters.55: It was not an enemy that reproached me, but a man mine equal. Oh that I had wings like a dove, for then would I fly away and be at rest.
chapters.56: Written when the Philistines took him in Gath. Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle.
chapters.57: In the cave. My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise.
chapters.58: A blunt psalm against corrupt judges, with the wicked compared to the deaf adder that stops her ear.
chapters.59: When Saul sent men to watch the house to kill him. Enemies who return at evening and make a noise like a dog.
chapters.60: After a military reverse. Thou hast shewed thy people hard things. Vain is the help of man.
chapters.61: Lead me to the rock that is higher than I. A prayer from the end of the earth.
chapters.62: Truly my soul waiteth upon God. Men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: laid in the balance they are lighter than vanity.
chapters.63: In the wilderness of Judah. My soul thirsteth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is.
chapters.64: Against the secret counsel of the wicked, who whet their tongue like a sword and shoot arrows of bitter words.
chapters.65: Praise for a good harvest. Thou crownest the year with thy goodness, and thy paths drop fatness.
chapters.66: Come and see the works of God. Thou broughtest us into the net; we went through fire and through water, but thou broughtest us out.
chapters.67: A short blessing psalm, echoing the priestly blessing of Numbers 6 and widening it to all nations.
chapters.68: A processional psalm of great difficulty and great energy. Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive.
chapters.69: Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul. They gave me gall and vinegar to drink — quoted at the crucifixion.
chapters.70: An urgent short psalm, almost identical to the closing verses of Psalm 40. Make haste unto me, O God.
chapters.71: A psalm of old age. Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth.
chapters.72: For Solomon. He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass. The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended.
chapters.73: Book Three opens with the problem of the prosperous wicked, unresolved until the writer went into the sanctuary.
chapters.74: A lament over the burning of the sanctuary, with axes breaking the carved work. We see not our signs; there is no more any prophet.
chapters.75: In the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red. Promotion cometh neither from the east nor from the west.
chapters.76: In Judah is God known. A psalm of a city delivered, with the stouthearted spoiled and sleeping their sleep.
chapters.77: Will the Lord cast off for ever? The turn comes with remembering the years of the right hand of the most High.
chapters.78: A long recital of national history from Egypt onward, told so that the generation to come might know.
chapters.79: The heathen are come into thine inheritance. A lament after the fall of Jerusalem, asking how long.
chapters.80: Turn us again, O God — a refrain repeated three times. Israel as a vine brought out of Egypt and now hedged down.
chapters.81: A feast psalm. Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it. Oh that my people had hearkened unto me.
chapters.82: God standing in the congregation of the mighty and judging the judges: defend the poor and fatherless.
chapters.83: A prayer against a coalition of nations named one by one, from Edom to Assyria.
chapters.84: How amiable are thy tabernacles. The sparrow hath found an house; a day in thy courts is better than a thousand.
chapters.85: Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
chapters.86: A prayer of David gathering lines from other psalms. Teach me thy way, O LORD; unite my heart to fear thy name.
chapters.87: Jerusalem as birthplace of the nations — even Rahab, Babylon, Philistia and Tyre counted as born there.
chapters.88: The darkest psalm in the book, ending with darkness as its last word and no resolution offered.
chapters.89: The covenant with David rehearsed at length, then set against a present disaster: thou hast cast off and abhorred.
chapters.90: A prayer of Moses, the oldest psalm by title. A thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday. Teach us to number our days.
chapters.91: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High. The snare of the fowler and the noisome pestilence; quoted at the temptation.
chapters.92: A psalm for the sabbath day. The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, and shall still bring forth fruit in old age.
chapters.93: The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty. The floods lift up their voice, but the LORD on high is mightier.
chapters.94: A cry for the God of vengeance to shew himself, on behalf of widows and strangers killed by those who say the LORD shall not see.
chapters.95: O come, let us sing unto the LORD — then a sharp turn: harden not your heart, as in the provocation. Quoted at length in Hebrews.
chapters.96: O sing unto the LORD a new song. Let the field be joyful, and all the trees of the wood rejoice before the LORD.
chapters.97: Clouds and darkness are round about him. The hills melted like wax at the presence of the LORD.
chapters.98: Let the floods clap their hands, let the hills be joyful together. The basis of the carol Joy to the World.
chapters.99: The LORD reigneth; let the people tremble. Moses, Aaron and Samuel named as those who called and were answered.
chapters.100: Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Enter into his gates with thanksgiving. Five verses, and among the best known.
chapters.101: A king's resolution about his own household: I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.
chapters.102: A penitential psalm of affliction. My days are consumed like smoke; I am like a pelican of the wilderness.
chapters.103: Bless the LORD, O my soul. As far as the east is from the west; as a father pitieth his children.
chapters.104: Creation surveyed — light as a garment, the springs among the hills, the young lions seeking their meat from God, and leviathan playing in the sea.
chapters.105: The history from Abraham to the conquest, told as reasons for thanksgiving.
chapters.106: The same history told as a confession of failure. We have sinned with our fathers. Book Four closes.
chapters.107: Book Five opens with four pictures of rescue — the lost traveller, the prisoner, the sick man, and those that go down to the sea in ships.
chapters.108: A psalm assembled from the endings of Psalms 57 and 60.
chapters.109: The most severe of the imprecatory psalms, calling down judgment on a betrayer; one verse is quoted of Judas in Acts 1.
chapters.110: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand. A priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. The most quoted psalm in the New Testament.
chapters.111: An acrostic of praise. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
chapters.112: A companion acrostic describing the man who fears the LORD: he shall not be afraid of evil tidings, his heart is fixed.
chapters.113: The first of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover. He raiseth up the poor out of the dust.
chapters.114: When Israel went out of Egypt. The sea saw it and fled; the mountains skipped like rams.
chapters.115: Not unto us, O LORD, but unto thy name give glory. Idols that have mouths but speak not, and those who make them made like them.
chapters.116: I love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
chapters.117: Two verses, the shortest chapter in the Bible, calling all nations to praise.
chapters.118: The last of the Hallel, sung on the way out of the upper room. The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
chapters.119: The longest chapter in the Bible: twenty-two stanzas of eight verses, one for each Hebrew letter, every verse on the word of God.
chapters.120: The first Song of Degrees, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech.
chapters.121: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills. The LORD is thy keeper; he that keepeth thee will not slumber.
chapters.122: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD. Pray for the peace of Jerusalem.
chapters.123: As the eyes of servants look unto the hand of their masters, so our eyes wait upon the LORD.
chapters.124: If it had not been the LORD who was on our side. Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers.
chapters.125: They that trust in the LORD shall be as mount Zion, which cannot be removed.
chapters.126: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth weeping shall doubtless come again with rejoicing.
chapters.127: Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Children are an heritage of the LORD.
chapters.128: A domestic blessing: thy wife as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house, thy children like olive plants.
chapters.129: The plowers plowed upon my back. Israel afflicted from her youth but not prevailed against.
chapters.130: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee. If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, who shall stand?
chapters.131: Three verses of quietness. I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother.
chapters.132: David's oath to find a place for the LORD, and the covenant answer: I will not turn from it.
chapters.133: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. The ointment running down Aaron's beard.
chapters.134: The last Song of Degrees, a night blessing for those who stand by night in the house of the LORD.
chapters.135: Praise gathered from other psalms, contrasting the God who does what he pleases with idols that cannot.
chapters.136: Every verse answered with the refrain: for his mercy endureth for ever. Twenty-six times.
chapters.137: By the rivers of Babylon we sat down and wept. How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land? It ends brutally.
chapters.138: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me. The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me.
chapters.139: Thou hast searched me, and known me. Whither shall I flee from thy presence? Fearfully and wonderfully made.
chapters.140: A prayer for preservation from violent men who have sharpened their tongues like a serpent.
chapters.141: Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth. Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness.
chapters.142: A prayer in the cave. Refuge failed me; no man cared for my soul.
chapters.143: The last of the seven penitential psalms. Enter not into judgment with thy servant, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified.
chapters.144: Blessed be the LORD my strength, which teacheth my hands to war. Man is like to vanity; his days are as a shadow.
chapters.145: An acrostic of praise. The LORD is good to all, and his tender mercies are over all his works.
chapters.146: The first of five closing Hallelujah psalms. Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
chapters.147: He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names. He giveth snow like wool.
chapters.148: Everything in creation called to praise in order — angels, sun and moon, sea monsters, fire and hail, beasts, kings and children.
chapters.149: A new song, with the high praises of God in their mouth and a twoedged sword in their hand.
chapters.150: Six verses of instruments — trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, organs, cymbals — ending: let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD.

books.name: Proverbs
books.scribe: Solomon chiefly (1:1; 10:1; 25:1), with sections by Agur (30) and King Lemuel (31). Chapters 25–29 were copied out later by Hezekiah's men.
books.summary: Practical wisdom in short lines: money, speech, work, friendship, sex, anger. Wisdom is personified as a woman calling in the street, and the fear of the LORD is where it starts.
laws: Honest weights and measures (11:1; 20:10)
Justice for the poor and the mute (31:8–9)
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Extended speeches urging a son to choose wisdom over the gang and the strange woman.
Hundreds of two-line contrasts on work, speech, money, temper.
Thirty sayings, including a warning against moving a landmark.
Copied out by the king's men two centuries later.
Numerical sayings, and the woman of valour acrostic.

chapters.1: The purpose stated, then the motto of the book: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. Wisdom cries in the streets and is ignored.
chapters.2: If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures. Wisdom as something worked for, not stumbled on.
chapters.3: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. Honour the LORD with thy substance.
chapters.4: A father passing on what his own father told him. Wisdom is the principal thing; keep thy heart with all diligence.
chapters.5: The first extended warning about the strange woman, whose lips drop as an honeycomb but whose end is bitter as wormwood.
chapters.6: Standing surety, the sluggard sent to the ant, and the six things the LORD hates, yea, seven are an abomination unto him.
chapters.7: A scene watched through a lattice: the young man void of understanding going the way to her house in the twilight.
chapters.8: Wisdom speaks for herself at the gates, and claims to have been set up from everlasting, rejoicing in the habitable part of the earth.
chapters.9: Two houses, two invitations. Wisdom has built her house and killed her beasts; the foolish woman calls from her door to the same passers-by.
chapters.10: The proverbs of Solomon begin: short two-line contrasts, wise against foolish, diligent against slothful, running for several chapters.
chapters.11: A false balance is abomination. The liberal soul shall be made fat, and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
chapters.12: The tongue throughout: a lying tongue is but for a moment, and there is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword.
chapters.13: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick. He that spareth his rod hateth his son.
chapters.14: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death. Righteousness exalteth a nation.
chapters.15: A soft answer turneth away wrath. Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
chapters.16: A man's heart deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps. Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
chapters.17: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity. A merry heart doeth good like a medicine.
chapters.18: The name of the LORD is a strong tower. He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
chapters.19: Better is the poor that walketh in his integrity than he that is perverse in his lips. He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD.
chapters.20: Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging. Divers weights and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination.
chapters.21: The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water. Better to dwell in a corner of the housetop.
chapters.22: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches. Train up a child in the way he should go. The words of the wise begin here.
chapters.23: Be not desirous of his dainties. Riches make themselves wings. Look not thou upon the wine when it is red — at the last it biteth like a serpent.
chapters.24: Be not thou envious against evil men. If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small. The field of the slothful, grown over with thorns.
chapters.25: These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah copied out. A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
chapters.26: The fool answered according and not according to his folly, and the sluggard turning on his bed as the door upon his hinges.
chapters.27: Boast not thyself of to morrow. Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
chapters.28: The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion. He that covereth his sins shall not prosper.
chapters.29: Where there is no vision, the people perish. A fool uttereth all his mind, but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
chapters.30: The words of Agur, built on numbered lists — four things that are never satisfied, four that are little upon the earth but exceeding wise.
chapters.31: King Lemuel repeating what his mother taught him, then the acrostic on the virtuous woman, whose price is far above rubies.

books.name: Ecclesiastes
books.scribe: 'The Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem' — traditionally Solomon in old age.
books.summary: A king with unlimited means tests pleasure, work, wisdom and wealth, and finds each one vapour. The conclusion is not despair but a narrowed life: eat your bread, do your work, fear God.
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Pleasure, building, wealth and wisdom all tested and weighed.
A time to every purpose; the oppression the Preacher keeps seeing.

moves.t: What wisdom can and cannot do
moves.n: Better-than sayings, and the limits of being clever.
Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth. Fear God and keep his commandments.

chapters.1: Vanity of vanities — the word means breath or vapour. One generation passeth away, and the earth abideth for ever. There is no new thing under the sun.
chapters.2: The Preacher tests pleasure, building, gardens, singers and wisdom itself, and finds all of it vexation of spirit.
chapters.3: To every thing there is a season. He hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh.
chapters.4: The tears of the oppressed with no comforter. Two are better than one; a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
chapters.5: Be not rash with thy mouth before God. He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver.
chapters.6: A man to whom God gives wealth and not the power to eat of it. Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire.
chapters.7: A good name is better than precious ointment. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting.
chapters.8: Who is as the wise man? A man's wisdom maketh his face to shine. Because sentence is not executed speedily, hearts are set to do evil.
chapters.9: One event happeneth to them all. Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might. A living dog is better than a dead lion.
chapters.10: Dead flies cause the ointment to send forth a stinking savour. Small follies outweigh reputation.
chapters.11: Cast thy bread upon the waters, for thou shalt find it after many days. He that observeth the wind shall not sow.
chapters.12: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, then old age in images — the grinders cease, the grasshopper is a burden. Fear God, and keep his commandments.

books.name: Song of Solomon
books.scribe: Solomon (1:1), who the text says wrote 1,005 songs — this being called the best of them.
books.summary: A love poem between a bride and her beloved, sung back and forth with a chorus of daughters of Jerusalem. Read plainly it is about desire and marriage; read allegorically, about God and his people.
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Longing, praise, and a search through the city at night.
The bridegroom's description of his bride; the garden shut up.
Mutual belonging, and the final claim that love is strong as death.

chapters.1: The bride speaks first. I am black, but comely. She asks where he feeds his flock at noon.
chapters.2: I am the rose of Sharon. The voice of the turtle is heard in our land. Take us the foxes, the little foxes.
chapters.3: By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth. Then Solomon's procession, with threescore valiant men about it.
chapters.4: Behold, thou art fair, my love — a description working downward. A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse.
chapters.5: I sleep, but my heart waketh. She rises too late, and the watchmen find and wound her.
chapters.6: Whither is thy beloved gone? Fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners.
chapters.7: A second description, this one upward from the feet, and the invitation to go forth into the field.
chapters.8: Set me as a seal upon thine heart: for love is strong as death. Many waters cannot quench love.

books.name: Isaiah
books.full: The Book of the Prophet Isaiah
books.scribe: Isaiah son of Amoz, prophet at the royal court in Jerusalem for about sixty years. Jewish tradition holds he was martyred under Manasseh. Some modern scholars divide the book between Isaiah and later disciples writing in his line; the book itself claims one prophet.
rulers: Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser and Sennacherib of Assyria
books.summary: Sixty-six chapters in two halves. Chapters 1–39 confront Judah under Assyrian threat; chapters 40–66 speak past that to exiles in Babylon who had not yet been taken, promising a return, a servant who suffers, and a new heavens and earth.
prophecies: Isa 7:14 — a virgin shall conceive
Isa 9:6 — unto us a child is born… The Prince of Peace
Isa 11:1 — a rod out of the stem of Jesse
Isa 44:28 and 45:1 — CYRUS NAMED as the shepherd who will say to Jerusalem, thou shalt be built
Isa 53 — the suffering servant wounded for our transgressions
Isa 65:17 — new heavens and a new earth
books.captivity: The north falls to Assyria in 722 during Isaiah's ministry. Babylon is named as the next captor a century before it happens.

moves.n: Judah indicted, Isaiah commissioned, Ahaz refuses a sign, a child is promised.
Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre — empire by empire.
The earth judged; death swallowed up in victory.
Six woes on those trusting Egypt instead of God; the highway of holiness.
Sennacherib's siege, Hezekiah's illness, and the Babylonian envoys.
Comfort ye my people; Cyrus named; four Servant Songs.
The scope widens to foreigners and eunuchs; new heavens and new earth.

chapters.1: Opening indictment. An ox knows its owner but Israel does not. God says he is sick of sacrifices offered by bloodstained hands — then offers the famous exchange: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.
chapters.2: A vision of the last days: nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD, swords beaten into plowshares. Then the reverse image — the day of the LORD against everything lofty, with men throwing their idols to the moles and bats.
chapters.3: Judah's leadership is stripped away — the judge, the soldier, the elder — and children are left to rule. A long, specific catalogue of the fashions of the women of Zion ends with the finery replaced by a rope and branding.
chapters.4: Short and hinged on hope. Seven women grab one man because the men are dead — but the branch of the LORD is beautiful, and a cloud and fire cover Zion as at Sinai.
chapters.5: The song of the vineyard: God planted it, tended it, and got wild grapes. Six woes follow — on land-grabbers, drunkards, those who call evil good, the self-wise, and corrupt judges.
chapters.6: THE CALL. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up, the seraphim crying holy, holy, holy. A coal touches his lips, he volunteers, and is told his preaching will harden rather than convert.
chapters.7: Ahaz is under siege from Syria and Israel. Isaiah brings his son Shear-jashub and tells the king to ask for a sign; Ahaz refuses in false piety, and the sign is given anyway — a virgin shall conceive, and shall call his name Immanuel.
chapters.8: The prophet's second son is given the longest name in the Bible, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, as a clock on Assyria's invasion. God is a sanctuary to some and a stone of stumbling to others.
chapters.9: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light. Unto us a child is born — Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. The chapter then turns to judgment on the north with a refrain that will not let go.
chapters.10: Assyria is God's axe, and does not know it. The chapter warns the axe against boasting over the one who swings it, and promises that a remnant shall return.
chapters.11: A rod out of the stem of Jesse, with the sevenfold Spirit resting on him — judging not by what his eyes see. Then the peaceable kingdom: wolf with lamb, and a child playing at the asp's hole.
chapters.12: A six-verse song of thanksgiving for the day of return. Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid.
chapters.13: The burden of BABYLON — named as the destroyer more than a century before it destroyed anything. It shall never be inhabited, and wild beasts shall lie there.
chapters.14: The taunt-song over the king of Babylon: how art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning. Oracles against Assyria and Philistia close the chapter.
chapters.15: The burden of Moab. A short, grieving oracle — the prophet says his own heart cries out for Moab, which is unusual in a judgment text.
chapters.16: Moab's oracle continues with an appeal for refuge and a three-year deadline. Isaiah says he will water it with his tears.
chapters.17: The burden of Damascus, which will cease from being a city. Israel is caught in the same sentence — nations rush like waters, and God rebukes them.
chapters.18: The land shadowing with wings, beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. Ambassadors are sent home; God watches from his dwelling place like clear heat, and prunes at the right moment.
chapters.19: The burden of EGYPT — civil war, dried-up Nile, confused counsellors. Then an astonishing turn: an altar to the LORD in the midst of Egypt, and a highway from Egypt to Assyria, with Israel a third with them.
chapters.20: Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years as a living sign that Egypt and Ethiopia will be led away stripped. One of the costliest sign-acts in scripture.
chapters.21: The burden of the desert of the sea. A watchman is posted; he reports Babylon is fallen, is fallen — a line Revelation will take up. Also oracles on Dumah and Arabia.
chapters.22: The valley of vision — Jerusalem itself. The city is on the rooftops celebrating while the enemy approaches; they reinforce the walls but do not look to God. Shebna the treasurer is demoted and Eliakim given the key of David.
chapters.23: The burden of TYRE, the merchant city. Its trade will stop for seventy years, then resume — and Isaiah says the merchandise will finally be holiness to the LORD.
chapters.24: The little apocalypse begins. The earth is turned upside down and its inhabitants scattered, priest and people alike; the earth reels like a drunkard under the weight of a broken everlasting covenant.
chapters.25: A song in the middle of the judgment. God spreads a feast of fat things for all people, swallows up death in victory, and wipes away tears from off all faces.
chapters.26: A song sung in the land of Judah. Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee. Also an early resurrection line — thy dead men shall live.
chapters.27: Leviathan is punished; the vineyard of red wine is now kept by God himself night and day. The scattered are gathered by a great trumpet.
chapters.28: Woe to the drunkards of Ephraim. The mocking teachers get precept upon precept, line upon line — and are told a foundation stone is laid in Zion, tried and precious.
chapters.29: Woe to Ariel, the city where David dwelt. The vision has become a sealed book nobody can read; the people draw near with their mouth while their heart is far away.
chapters.30: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help. Yet the LORD waits to be gracious, and a voice behind them says: this is the way, walk ye in it.
chapters.31: A short reprise of the same warning — the Egyptians are men and not God, their horses flesh and not spirit.
chapters.32: A king shall reign in righteousness, and every man be as a hiding place from the wind. The women at ease are shaken, until the Spirit is poured from on high and the wilderness becomes a field.
chapters.33: Woe to the treacherous spoiler. The question is asked: who among us shall dwell with devouring fire? The answer is a moral one, and the chapter ends with the LORD as judge, lawgiver and king.
chapters.34: Judgment on the nations, with Edom singled out. The imagery is total — the heavens rolled together as a scroll.
chapters.35: The desert shall rejoice and blossom as the rose. Eyes opened, ears unstopped, the lame man leaping — and a highway called the way of holiness, where no lion goes.
chapters.36: HISTORY BEGINS. Sennacherib's field commander stands outside Jerusalem's wall and delivers a propaganda speech in Hebrew so the soldiers on the wall can hear it.
chapters.37: Hezekiah takes the threatening letter into the Temple and spreads it before the LORD. Isaiah answers; the angel of the LORD strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib goes home and is murdered by his sons.
chapters.38: Hezekiah is told to set his house in order, prays, weeps, and is given fifteen more years — confirmed by the shadow going back ten degrees. His written psalm of recovery is included.
chapters.39: THE HINGE OF THE BOOK. Hezekiah shows Babylonian envoys everything in his treasury, and Isaiah tells him it will all be carried to Babylon, and his sons made eunuchs there. Hezekiah's reply is that at least there will be peace in his own days.
chapters.40: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people. A voice cries in the wilderness; all flesh is grass; the nations are a drop in a bucket. It closes with those who wait upon the LORD mounting up with wings as eagles.
chapters.41: God calls the nations into court to argue their case. Fear thou not, for I am with thee — I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness. Idols are challenged to predict anything at all.
chapters.42: THE FIRST SERVANT SONG. Behold my servant, whom I uphold — a bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench. He is given as a covenant to the people and a light to the Gentiles.
chapters.43: Fear not, for I have redeemed thee; when thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee. God announces he is doing a new thing, and blots out transgressions for his own sake.
chapters.44: An extended satire on idol-making: a man cuts a tree, burns half for warmth, roasts meat over it, and worships the rest. The chapter closes by naming CYRUS as the one who will say to Jerusalem, thou shalt be built.
chapters.45: God addresses Cyrus by name as his anointed, saying he girded him though Cyrus did not know him. I form the light and create darkness. Every knee shall bow — a line Paul will quote twice.
chapters.46: Bel bows and Nebo stoops. The idols must be carried by their worshippers; God says he has carried Israel from the belly and will carry it to old age and grey hairs.
chapters.47: The fall of Babylon addressed as a woman losing her throne. Her astrologers and monthly prognosticators are told to stand up and save her, and cannot.
chapters.48: God says he told them beforehand precisely so they could not credit their idols. O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments — then had thy peace been as a river.
chapters.49: THE SECOND SERVANT SONG. Called from the womb, given as a light to the Gentiles that he may be salvation to the ends of the earth. Zion says God has forgotten her; the answer is a mother forgetting her nursing child.
chapters.50: THE THIRD SERVANT SONG. The servant gives his back to the smiters and his cheeks to those who pluck out the hair. He is not confounded, having set his face like a flint.
chapters.51: Look to the rock whence ye are hewn. Jerusalem is told to wake up, having drunk the cup of trembling to its dregs — and the cup is taken out of her hand.
chapters.52: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings. The last three verses open the fourth Servant Song: his visage was so marred more than any man.
chapters.53: THE SUFFERING SERVANT. Despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities. He opened not his mouth. He made his grave with the wicked — and shall see his seed and prolong his days.
chapters.54: Sing, O barren. The tent is enlarged and the stakes strengthened. God calls his anger a small moment and swears by the waters of Noah never to be wroth in that way again.
chapters.55: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters. My thoughts are not your thoughts — and the word that goes out of God's mouth shall not return void.
chapters.56: The scope widens dramatically: foreigners and eunuchs, previously excluded from the assembly, are promised a name better than sons and daughters. Mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.
chapters.57: A rebuke of idolatry conducted under every green tree, alongside the line that the righteous perishes and no man lays it to heart. God dwells with the humble and contrite.
chapters.58: The fast God chooses is not bowed heads and sackcloth but loosing the bands of wickedness, feeding the hungry, and housing the poor. Also the promise attached to keeping the sabbath.
chapters.59: Your iniquities have separated between you and your God. A blunt confession of national injustice — and God, seeing no intercessor, puts on righteousness as a breastplate himself.
chapters.60: Arise, shine, for thy light is come. Nations and kings come to the brightness of thy rising; gold and incense are brought, gates stay open day and night, and the sun is no longer needed.
chapters.61: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek — the passage Jesus read at Nazareth, stopping mid-verse. Beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning.
chapters.62: Jerusalem is renamed — no more Forsaken and Desolate, but Hephzibah and Beulah. Watchmen are set on the walls who are told not to keep silent.
chapters.63: The figure treading the winepress alone, garments stained red. Then a long remembrance of God's mercies of old, and a plea: doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us.
chapters.64: The prayer continues — oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens and come down. We are all as an unclean thing, and our righteousnesses as filthy rags. Yet thou art the potter, and we are the clay.
chapters.65: God answers: I am found of them that sought me not. Judgment on the idolaters, then the creation of new heavens and a new earth, where the infant does not die and men enjoy the work of their hands.
chapters.66: The closing chapter. Heaven is God's throne — where is the house you build me? He looks instead to the poor and contrite. Zion gives birth in a day, the nations are gathered to see his glory, and the book ends on both the new heavens and an unquenched fire.

books.name: Jeremiah
books.full: The Book of the Prophet Jeremiah
books.scribe: Jeremiah of Anathoth, a priest's son, dictating to BARUCH the son of Neriah, who wrote the scroll (36:4) — rewrote it after King Jehoiakim burned it (36:32).
rulers: ZEDEKIAH, the last king of Judah
books.summary: Forty years of warning nobody wanted, delivered while the city was actually falling. Jeremiah is beaten, jailed in a cistern, and finally dragged to Egypt — and told to buy a field as a sign that the land would be lived in again.
prophecies: Jer 25:11–12 — SEVENTY YEARS of Babylonian service, then Babylon punished
Jer 29:10 — after seventy years I will visit you and cause you to return
Jer 31:31–34 — a new covenant written in the heart
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN. Jeremiah lives through all three deportations and the burning of the Temple.

moves.t: The call and the early warnings
moves.n: A prophet from before birth; the almond rod, the potter's wheel, the Temple sermon.
Plots on his life, and Jeremiah's bitter complaints to God.
The line of Judah's last kings, and the letter promising seventy years.
The new covenant, and a field bought while the army is at the gate.
The scroll burned, the cistern, the city taken.
Oracles against nine nations, and an appendix on the fall.

chapters.1: Jeremiah is called as a boy and told he was appointed before he was born. He protests that he cannot speak; the answer is an almond rod and a boiling pot tilted from the north.
chapters.2: The first oracle: Israel is charged with exchanging living water for cracked cisterns that hold none. The marriage imagery that runs through the book begins here.
chapters.3: Backsliding Israel and treacherous Judah compared. Judah is the worse of the two, having watched the north fall and learned nothing. Yet the call is still 'return'.
chapters.4: A northern invader is announced. Jeremiah sees the land reverting to the formlessness of Genesis 1 — without form and void, the light gone from the heavens.
chapters.5: Search Jerusalem for one just man. The prophets prophesy falsely, the priests rule by their means, and the people love to have it so.
chapters.6: The siege is drawn up in detail. The wound of the daughter of the people is healed slightly, with cries of peace where there is no peace.
chapters.7: The Temple sermon, delivered in the gate. Do not trust in the words 'the temple of the LORD' — go and see what happened at Shiloh. It nearly costs him his life in chapter 26.
chapters.8: No peace, and the harvest is past. The stork and the crane know their appointed times; the people do not know the judgment of the LORD.
chapters.9: The lament: oh that my head were waters. Wisdom, might and riches are all set aside — only knowing the LORD is worth glorying in.
chapters.10: Idols mocked as scarecrows in a cucumber field, upright as the palm tree but unable to speak or walk. Set against the God who made the earth by his power.
chapters.11: The broken covenant. A conspiracy is found among the men of Anathoth, Jeremiah's own town, who tell him to stop prophesying or die.
chapters.12: Jeremiah's complaint: why does the way of the wicked prosper? The answer is not comfort but escalation — if footmen have wearied you, how will you run with horses?
chapters.13: The linen girdle buried by the Euphrates and dug up marred. A sign of a people meant to cling to God and left to rot.
chapters.14: Drought, and the prophets who promise peace. God forbids Jeremiah to pray for this people — one of the hardest verses in the book.
chapters.15: A second complaint, and the sharpest reply: if Moses and Samuel stood before me, my mind could not be toward this people. Jeremiah is told to repent of his own bitterness.
chapters.16: Jeremiah is forbidden to marry, to mourn, or to feast. His whole life becomes the sign — no household to lose, no funerals to attend.
chapters.17: The heart is deceitful above all things. Set against the man who trusts in the LORD, a tree planted by the waters that does not fear the drought.
chapters.18: The potter's house. The clay is marred and remade; the point is that a nation's future is not fixed, and either promise or threat can be reversed by repentance.
chapters.19: A potter's earthen bottle broken in the valley of Hinnom before the elders. Unlike wet clay, a fired vessel cannot be remade — the window has closed.
chapters.20: Pashur the priest puts Jeremiah in the stocks. He emerges with the most bitter passage in the prophets: cursed be the day wherein I was born.
chapters.21: Zedekiah sends to enquire, hoping for a miracle. The answer is that God himself is fighting against the city, and the way of life is surrender.
chapters.22: Judgment on four kings in turn: Shallum, Jehoiakim, Coniah. Jehoiakim will be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn out beyond the gates.
chapters.23: Against the shepherds who scatter the flock, and the prophets who steal words from one another. The BRANCH of righteousness is promised in the middle of it.
chapters.24: Two baskets of figs. The good figs are the exiles already in Babylon; the bad are those left in Jerusalem who think they escaped.
chapters.25: Seventy years is named. The cup of the wine of wrath is passed to all the nations in turn, beginning at Jerusalem and ending at Sheshach.
chapters.26: The Temple sermon retold from the outside: Jeremiah is seized and tried for his life. Elders cite the precedent of Micah, and he is spared; Urijah is not.
chapters.27: Yokes of wood sent to the surrounding kings. Serve Babylon and live — counsel that sounded like treason and was meant literally.
chapters.28: Hananiah breaks Jeremiah's yoke and promises return within two years. Jeremiah answers with a yoke of iron, and Hananiah dies that year.
chapters.29: The letter to the exiles: build houses, plant gardens, seek the peace of the city. The famous promise of a future and a hope is addressed to people told to settle in.
chapters.30: The Book of Consolation opens. Jacob's trouble is real, but it is the trouble of a birth, not a death.
chapters.31: The new covenant, written on the heart rather than on stone. Rachel weeping for her children, and the promise that they will come again from the land of the enemy.
chapters.32: With the siege works already built, Jeremiah buys a field at Anathoth and files the deed in an earthen vessel. Houses and fields shall be possessed again in this land.
chapters.33: Further promise: the voice of the bridegroom will be heard again in streets now desolate. The covenant with David is set as firm as day and night.
chapters.34: Zedekiah frees the Hebrew slaves during the siege, then takes them back when the pressure lifts. The broken oath is judged in the terms of the covenant ceremony itself.
chapters.35: The Rechabites refuse wine because their ancestor told them not to. Their obedience to a human father is set against Judah's disregard of God.
chapters.36: Baruch writes the scroll at dictation; Jehoiakim cuts it column by column and burns it. Jeremiah dictates it again, with many like words added.
chapters.37: Jeremiah tries to leave the city on family business and is arrested as a deserter. Zedekiah interviews him secretly, hoping the message has changed. It has not.
chapters.38: Lowered into a miry dungeon and left to sink. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian gets him out with rags and old cast clouts to spare his arms.
chapters.39: The city falls. Zedekiah's sons are killed before him, then his eyes are put out. Jeremiah is released by the Babylonians and treated well.
chapters.40: Gedaliah is appointed governor and counsels submission. Warned of a plot against him, he refuses to believe it.
chapters.41: Ishmael murders Gedaliah at a meal, kills eighty pilgrims, and throws the bodies into a pit. The last fragile order collapses.
chapters.42: The remnant swears to obey whatever answer comes, then waits ten days for it. The answer is: stay in the land, do not go to Egypt.
chapters.43: They go to Egypt anyway and take Jeremiah with them. He hides stones at Tahpanhes where Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne.
chapters.44: The last recorded oracle. The people answer plainly that they will keep burning incense to the queen of heaven, because things went better when they did.
chapters.45: A short word to Baruch, who wanted great things for himself. He is promised his life as a prize of war, and nothing else.
chapters.46: Oracles against the nations begin with Egypt, and Pharaoh Necho's defeat at Carchemish.
chapters.47: Against the Philistines, before Pharaoh smote Gaza.
chapters.48: Against Moab, the longest of the foreign oracles. Moab has been at ease from his youth, settled on his lees, never emptied from vessel to vessel.
chapters.49: Against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Elam in turn.
chapters.50: Against Babylon, the instrument now judged in its turn. Israel is a scattered sheep driven away by lions.
chapters.51: Babylon's fall continued. Seraiah is told to read the scroll aloud in Babylon, tie a stone to it, and throw it into the Euphrates.
chapters.52: A historical appendix, largely parallel to 2 Kings 25. The Temple furnishings are inventoried as they are carried off, and Jehoiachin is released from prison at the end.

books.name: Lamentations
books.scribe: Jeremiah, by tradition — the KJV title says so outright. Five poems, four of them acrostics running through the Hebrew alphabet.
books.written: c. 586 BC, immediately after the fall
rulers: No king — Zedekiah blinded and deported
books.summary: Five funeral poems for a burned city, written by someone who watched it happen. The centre of the middle poem contains the line about mercies new every morning — placed exactly at the structural heart.
themes: Mercy in the middle of ruin
prophecies: Lam 3:22–23 — his compassions fail not, they are new every morning
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — written in the smoke.

moves.n: An acrostic lament for a widowed capital.
The unbearable claim that God did this.

moves.t: The man who has seen affliction
moves.n: A triple acrostic — and at its centre, mercies new every morning.
Gold dimmed; the horror of the siege recounted plainly.
Not an acrostic. Turn thou us unto thee, and we shall be turned.

chapters.1: How doth the city sit solitary. An acrostic — twenty-two stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter. Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?
chapters.2: The LORD himself named as the one who did it: he hath swallowed up Israel, and bent his bow like an enemy.
chapters.3: The middle chapter, and a triple acrostic — three verses per letter. At its centre: his compassions fail not, they are new every morning.
chapters.4: How is the gold become dim. The precious sons of Zion compared to earthen pitchers, and the horrors of the siege recorded plainly.
chapters.5: The only chapter that is not an acrostic, and it reads like a prayer that has run out of form. Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned.

books.name: Ezekiel
books.full: The Book of the Prophet Ezekiel
books.scribe: Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest deported in the second wave, prophesying by the river Chebar in Babylon. He dates his own visions precisely, to the day.
books.summary: A priest who never got to serve in a temple, given visions of one. Wheels and living creatures, a valley of dry bones, and a measured blueprint for a house that has not been built.
prophecies: Ezek 36:26 — a new heart and a new spirit
Ezek 37 — the dry bones: these bones are the whole house of Israel
Ezek 40–48 — the measured temple and the river from the threshold
laws: Ezek 18 — the soul that sinneth, it shall die: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — he was taken in the 597 deportation.

moves.n: The wheels, the living creatures, the scroll he is made to eat.
Sign-acts: a brick, shaved hair, a packed bag; the glory leaves the Temple.
Seven nations, with Tyre and Egypt at length.
The watchman, the shepherds, the dry bones, Gog.
Measured to the cubit, with a river rising from the door.

chapters.1: By the river Chebar in exile, the vision of the whirlwind, the four living creatures and the wheels within wheels. The glory of God is mobile — it has come to Babylon.
chapters.2: Ezekiel is commissioned and addressed throughout as son of man. He is sent to a rebellious house, whether they hear or forbear.
chapters.3: He eats the scroll and it is sweet as honey. Made a watchman, warned that the blood of the unwarned will be required at his hand.
chapters.4: The siege enacted in miniature on a tile, with an iron pan for a wall. He lies on one side for the years of Israel's guilt, then the other for Judah's.
chapters.5: Hair shaved with a sword, weighed and divided in thirds — burned, struck, scattered. Jerusalem set in the midst of the nations and judged in their sight.
chapters.6: Against the mountains of Israel and the high places, where the altars will be broken and the bones scattered around them.
chapters.7: An end is come upon the four corners of the land. Silver and gold will be cast into the streets, unable to buy bread.
chapters.8: Carried in vision to the Temple and shown what happens inside it: creeping things portrayed on the walls, women weeping for Tammuz, men bowing to the sun.
chapters.9: The man with the writer's inkhorn marks the foreheads of those who sigh for the abominations. The slaughter begins at the sanctuary.
chapters.10: The glory of the LORD moves from the threshold to the cherubim and the wheels. Coals of fire are scattered over the city.
chapters.11: Judgment on the counsellors, and the promise of a heart of flesh for a heart of stone. The glory departs and stands upon the mountain east of the city.
chapters.12: Ezekiel digs through the wall and carries out his baggage at evening, covering his face. The prince will do the same and not see the land with his eyes.
chapters.13: Against prophets who daub the wall with untempered mortar, and against women who sew pillows to armholes to hunt souls.
chapters.14: Elders come to enquire with idols in their hearts. Even Noah, Daniel and Job in this land could deliver only their own souls.
chapters.15: The vine parable. Vine wood is useless for anything but burning; that is the point of the comparison, not fruitfulness.
chapters.16: Jerusalem as a foundling raised to be a queen and turned harlot. The most graphic chapter in the prophets, ending nonetheless in an everlasting covenant.
chapters.17: The riddle of two eagles and a vine — Nebuchadnezzar, Egypt, and Zedekiah's broken oath. A tender twig will be planted on a high mountain.
chapters.18: The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The proverb about fathers eating sour grapes is retired: no one inherits guilt, and no one is fixed in their past.
chapters.19: A lamentation for the princes of Israel, sung as a dirge about a lioness and her whelps, and a vine plucked up in fury.
chapters.20: The elders enquire again; the answer is a history of rebellion from Egypt onward, and a refusal to be enquired of.
chapters.21: The song of the sword, sharpened and furbished. The king of Babylon stands at the parting of the way and uses divination to choose Jerusalem.
chapters.22: The bloody city catalogued: princes like wolves, prophets daubing, priests violating the law. God sought for a man to stand in the gap and found none.
chapters.23: Aholah and Aholibah, Samaria and Jerusalem, two sisters whose foreign alliances are described as prostitution. A companion piece to chapter 16.
chapters.24: The boiling pot with its scum, and the death of Ezekiel's wife, the desire of his eyes, whom he is forbidden to mourn. The same day the siege begins.
chapters.25: Oracles against Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia, all judged for rejoicing at Jerusalem's fall.
chapters.26: Against Tyre, which said Aha against Jerusalem. The city will be scraped bare, a place for the spreading of nets.
chapters.27: The lament over Tyre as a splendid ship, with an inventory of her trade from every quarter, wrecked in the midst of the seas.
chapters.28: Against the prince of Tyre, whose heart is lifted up as the heart of God. The lament that follows, set in Eden and on the holy mountain, has long been read as reaching past the man.
chapters.29: Against Egypt and Pharaoh, the great dragon in the midst of his rivers, who said My river is mine own and I have made it.
chapters.30: The day of the LORD upon Egypt, with her allies falling by the sword and the arms of Pharaoh broken.
chapters.31: Assyria as a cedar in Lebanon, taller than all the trees, cut down as a warning to Egypt.
chapters.32: A lamentation for Pharaoh, and a descent into the pit where the fallen nations lie in ranks with their weapons under their heads.
chapters.33: The watchman charge repeated, and the news arrives: the city is smitten. From here the book turns from judgment to restoration.
chapters.34: Against the shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock. God will search out the sheep himself and set one shepherd over them.
chapters.35: Against mount Seir and Edom, for perpetual hatred and for shedding the blood of Israel in the time of their calamity.
chapters.36: The mountains of Israel addressed directly and promised people again. A new heart and a new spirit, and God acting for his own name's sake.
chapters.37: The valley of dry bones: can these bones live? Sinews, flesh and breath in stages. Then two sticks joined into one in the hand.
chapters.38: Gog of the land of Magog comes up against a land of unwalled villages, and is drawn there by God himself.
chapters.39: Gog's fall; seven years of weapons for fuel, and seven months of burial. Israel will know the LORD from that day forward.
chapters.40: The vision of the new Temple begins, measured in cubits by a man with a line of flax and a measuring reed.
chapters.41: The measurements of the house itself, the holy place and the most holy, with cherubim and palm trees carved on every wall.
chapters.42: The chambers for the priests, and the wall separating the sanctuary from the profane place.
chapters.43: The glory returns by the east gate — the way it left in chapter 10. The altar is measured and its consecration prescribed.
chapters.44: The east gate is shut because the LORD entered by it. Duties are divided between the sons of Zadok and the Levites who went astray.
chapters.45: The holy portion of land set apart, and just balances required of the princes: a just ephah and a just bath.
chapters.46: The prince's offerings, and the rule that worshippers leave by the opposite gate from the one they entered.
chapters.47: Waters issue from under the threshold, ankle deep, then knees, then loins, then waters to swim in. Everything lives where the river comes.
chapters.48: The land divided among the tribes in parallel strips, and the city's twelve gates named. The last words: the LORD is there.

books.name: Daniel
books.scribe: Daniel, taken to Babylon as a youth of the royal seed and trained for the king's service. Chapters 1–6 are told about him; 7–12 are written in the first person.
books.summary: Six chapters of court survival and six of vision, spanning seventy years and three empires. Daniel outlasts the kingdom that captured him and is still in office when Cyrus lets the exiles go.
prophecies: Dan 2 — the image of gold, silver, brass and iron: four kingdoms and a stone cut without hands
Dan 7 — four beasts and one like the Son of man given an everlasting dominion
Dan 8 — the ram and the he-goat, named as Media-Persia and Greece
Dan 9:24–27 — the seventy weeks
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN, from the first deportation of 605 to the Persian release.

moves.n: The diet, the dream, the furnace, the writing on the wall, the lions.
Four beasts, ram and goat, seventy weeks, and a final long revelation.

chapters.1: Nebuchadnezzar's first deportation, 605 BC. Four young captives of royal blood are enrolled in a three-year Babylonian education. Daniel asks for pulse and water instead of the king's meat, and proposes a ten-day trial.
chapters.2: The king demands his wise men tell him the dream as well as its meaning, on pain of death. Daniel describes the image of gold, silver, brass and iron with feet of clay — four kingdoms — and a stone cut without hands that becomes a mountain.
chapters.3: The golden image on the plain of Dura and an orchestra as the signal to bow. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego answer that God is able to deliver them, but if not, they still will not bow. A fourth figure walks in the furnace.
chapters.4: Nebuchadnezzar's own account, written in the first person as a public proclamation. A tree cut down, seven times passing over him, and a king who eats grass like an ox until he lifts his eyes to heaven.
chapters.5: Belshazzar's feast, using the vessels taken from the Temple. A hand writes on the plaster: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. Daniel reads it as counted, weighed, divided — and Babylon falls that night.
chapters.6: A new empire, and a law that no petition may be made to anyone but the king for thirty days. Daniel opens his windows toward Jerusalem and prays as he did before. The lions' den, and Darius fasting all night.
chapters.7: The visions begin. Four beasts out of the sea — lion, bear, leopard, and a dreadful fourth with ten horns. The Ancient of days sits, and one like the Son of man is given a dominion that shall not pass away.
chapters.8: A ram and a he-goat, and the angel Gabriel names them outright: the ram is Media and Persia, the goat is Greece. The little horn that follows, and the 2,300 days.
chapters.9: Daniel reads Jeremiah and works out that the seventy years are nearly up. His prayer of confession is interrupted by Gabriel with the vision of SEVENTY WEEKS — the most debated timeline in scripture.
chapters.10: A three-week fast by the river Hiddekel, and a vision that leaves him with no strength. A messenger explains he was withstood twenty-one days by the prince of the kingdom of Persia.
chapters.11: The most detailed predictive chapter in the Old Testament — kings of the north and south in sequence, matching the Ptolemies and Seleucids so closely that its dating is a standing argument among scholars.
chapters.12: The close: a time of trouble such as never was, many that sleep in the dust awakening, and Daniel told to shut up the words and seal the book. Go thy way till the end be, for thou shalt rest.

books.name: Hosea
books.scribe: Hosea son of Beeri, prophet to the northern kingdom — the only writing prophet native to the north.
rulers: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah
books.summary: God tells a prophet to marry a woman who will be unfaithful, and then to take her back, so the nation can see its own marriage from the outside. The last of the northern prophets before 722.
prophecies: Hos 3:4–5 — Israel shall abide many days without a king and without a sacrifice
Hos 11:1 — out of Egypt have I called my son
books.captivity: Writes on the edge of the ASSYRIAN deportation of the north.

moves.n: Gomer, three children with prophetic names, and a purchase back.
Israel's unfaithfulness spelled out — and God's refusal to give up.

chapters.1: Hosea is told to marry a wife of whoredoms. Three children named as sentences: Jezreel, Loruhamah (not pitied) and Loammi (not my people).
chapters.2: The charge against the mother, then the turn — I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her.
chapters.3: He buys her back for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley, and tells her to abide for him many days.
chapters.4: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. The priests share the blame: they eat up the sin of my people.
chapters.5: Judgment on priest, people and king alike. I will be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness.
chapters.6: Come, and let us return. But their goodness is as a morning cloud. I desired mercy, and not sacrifice — quoted twice by Jesus.
chapters.7: Ephraim is a cake not turned — burnt on one side and raw on the other. A silly dove without heart, calling to Egypt and Assyria.
chapters.8: They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. The calf of Samaria named and rejected.
chapters.9: The days of visitation are come. Israel shall know it; the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad.
chapters.10: Break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD. Israel as an empty vine bringing forth fruit unto himself.
chapters.11: The most tender chapter: when Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt. I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms.
chapters.12: Jacob recalled — he took his brother by the heel, and by his strength he had power with God. A merchant with balances of deceit.
chapters.13: I will be thy plagues, O death; I will be thy destruction, O grave. Quoted by Paul on the resurrection.
chapters.14: The closing appeal: take with you words, and turn to the LORD. I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.

books.name: Joel
books.scribe: Joel son of Pethuel. Undated in the text — estimates run from the ninth century to after the exile.
rulers: Uncertain — the book names no king, which is itself a clue
books.summary: A locust plague strips the land bare, and the prophet reads it as a rehearsal for the day of the LORD. Then a promise: the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
prophecies: Joel 2:28–32 — I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, quoted by Peter at Pentecost
laws: Fasting and solemn assembly called (1:14; 2:15)
books.captivity: None named.

moves.n: Four waves strip everything; a call to fast.
An army like locusts — and then the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
The valley of decision; plowshares beaten into swords.

chapters.1: A locust plague described in waves — palmerworm, locust, cankerworm, caterpiller. Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell theirs.
chapters.2: Blow the trumpet in Zion. The locusts become an army, then the call: rend your heart, and not your garments. I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.
chapters.3: The nations gathered into the valley of Jehoshaphat. Beat your plowshares into swords — Isaiah's image deliberately reversed.

books.name: Amos
books.scribe: Amos of Tekoa, a herdsman and dresser of sycomore fruit — not a professional prophet, and he says so (7:14).
rulers: Amaziah, priest of Bethel, who tries to deport him
books.summary: A southern farmer walks north into a boom economy and tells it that its prosperity is built on crushed people. Eight oracles circle the neighbours before landing on Israel itself.
themes: The day of the LORD as darkness
prophecies: Amos 8:11 — a famine of hearing the words of the LORD
Amos 9:11 — I will raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen
laws: Amos 5:24 — let judgment run down as waters
Condemnation of false balances and selling the poor for shoes (8:5–6)
books.captivity: Predicts deportation beyond Damascus — fulfilled in 722.

moves.n: Six neighbours indicted, then Judah, then Israel itself.
Privilege means accountability; luxury built on the poor.
Locusts, fire, plumbline, summer fruit, the Lord at the altar — and a final restoration.

chapters.1: For three transgressions and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof — the same formula against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre and Edom in turn.
chapters.2: The circle closes on Moab, then Judah, then Israel itself, who sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes.
chapters.3: Can two walk together, except they be agreed? A herdsman's logic: the lion hath roared, who will not fear?
chapters.4: I have given you cleanness of teeth in all your cities — five judgments, each ending yet have ye not returned unto me. Prepare to meet thy God.
chapters.5: Seek ye me, and ye shall live. I hate, I despise your feast days. Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
chapters.6: Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, that lie upon beds of ivory and chant to the sound of the viol, but are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph.
chapters.7: Locusts and fire withdrawn at Amos's intercession, then the plumbline, which is not. Amaziah tells him to go back to Judah and prophesy for bread there.
chapters.8: A basket of summer fruit, and a pun on the word for end. A famine, not of bread, but of hearing the words of the LORD.
chapters.9: I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve. Then the tabernacle of David raised up, quoted at the Jerusalem council.

books.name: Obadiah
books.scribe: Obadiah — nothing else is known of him. The shortest book in the Old Testament, 21 verses.
books.summary: One oracle against Edom, the nation descended from Esau, for standing at the crossroads and cheering while Jerusalem burned. Pride in a rock fortress does not save it.
prophecies: Obad 15 — as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — written in its aftermath.

moves.n: Twenty-one verses: pride in the rock, betrayal of a brother, the day of the LORD.

chapters.1: Twenty-one verses against Edom, Jacob's brother, for standing on the other side while strangers carried away his substance. The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee.

books.name: Jonah
books.scribe: Jonah son of Amittai, named in 2 Kgs 14:25 as a prophet under Jeroboam II. The book is written about him, not by him.
rulers: the king of Nineveh, capital of Assyria
books.summary: A prophet is sent to the capital of the empire that will destroy his country, runs the opposite way, and is furious when the city repents. The book ends on a question God asks him.
prophecies: Jon 1:17 — three days and three nights, cited by Christ as a sign (Mt 12:40)
books.captivity: None yet — Nineveh spared here destroys Israel forty years later.

moves.n: To Joppa, to Tarshish, into the hold, into the sea.
A prayer from the fish's belly, quoting the Psalms.
Eight words of preaching, and a city of 120,000 repents.
A gourd, a worm, a hot wind, and God's closing question.

chapters.1: Sent to Nineveh, he goes to Joppa and pays the fare to Tarshish. The sailors pray while he sleeps, and cast him out at his own suggestion.
chapters.2: A psalm prayed from the fish's belly, quoting other psalms almost throughout. Salvation is of the LORD.
chapters.3: The second commission, and the shortest sermon on record. The whole city repents, from the king down to the cattle.
chapters.4: Jonah is angry that God relented, which is what he feared all along. A gourd, a worm, and the last question, which is never answered.

books.name: Micah
books.scribe: Micah the Morasthite, from a farming town in the Judean lowlands — a contemporary of Isaiah with a very different vantage point.
books.summary: Three cycles of doom and hope, from a country prophet who names the corruption of judges, priests and prophets who take money. He is quoted a century later in Jeremiah's defence trial.
prophecies: Mic 3:12 — Zion shall be plowed as a field
Mic 5:2 — BETHLEHEM EPHRATAH, out of thee shall he come forth
laws: Mic 6:8 — to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God
books.captivity: Names both the Assyrian threat and a Babylonian exile (4:10).

moves.n: Samaria and Jerusalem indicted; land seized by those with power to seize it.
Corrupt leaders — and Bethlehem named as the birthplace of the ruler.
