God's lawsuit against his people; what doth the LORD require of thee.

chapters.1: Hear, all ye people. Judgment on both capitals, Samaria and Jerusalem, with a run of puns on the names of the towns in his own district.
chapters.2: Woe to them that devise iniquity upon their beds, and covet fields and take them by violence.
chapters.3: Rulers who hate the good and love the evil, and prophets who cry peace if they are fed. Zion shall be plowed as a field.
chapters.4: The mountain of the house of the LORD established, and swords beaten into plowshares — the same oracle as Isaiah 2.
chapters.5: But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah. Cited by the scribes to Herod.
chapters.6: The LORD's controversy with his people, put as a lawsuit. What doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
chapters.7: The good man is perished out of the earth. Yet the ending: who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and casteth their sins into the depths of the sea.

books.name: Nahum
books.scribe: Nahum the Elkoshite. Nothing more is known of him.
books.summary: The sequel to Jonah, 150 years on. Nineveh repented once; now the verdict is final. The city fell in 612 BC, and the book reads like a report filed in advance.
themes: Justice deferred is not justice denied
prophecies: Nah 1:8 and 3:19 — an overrunning flood shall make an utter end of the place
books.power: Assyria at its peak, about to collapse
books.captivity: The north is already gone.

moves.n: Slow to anger, great in power — and a stronghold in trouble.
The attack described as if watched from the wall.
The city that made others childless; there is no healing of thy bruise.

chapters.1: The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power. The same God who is a strong hold in the day of trouble makes an utter end of Nineveh.
chapters.2: The siege in fast, clipped lines — the chariots raging in the streets, the shields of the mighty men made red.
chapters.3: Woe to the bloody city. Nahum points to No, the Egyptian capital that also fell, and asks why Nineveh should be different.

books.name: Habakkuk
books.scribe: Habakkuk — the only prophet whose book is structured as an argument with God rather than a message to people.
books.summary: The prophet asks why God tolerates injustice in Judah, and is told he is raising up the Chaldeans — which is worse. Chapter 3 is his answer: a psalm sung while the fig tree fails.
prophecies: Hab 2:4 — the just shall live by his faith, quoted three times in the New Testament
Hab 1:6 — I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation
books.captivity: Predicts the BABYLONIAN invasion just before it arrives.

moves.n: Why do you tolerate this? — and the answer Habakkuk did not want.
The just shall live by his faith; woes on plunder, greed and idols.
A psalm with musical notation: though the fig tree shall not blossom.

chapters.1: The prophet complains that God does nothing about violence. The answer is worse than the silence: I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation.
chapters.2: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables. The just shall live by his faith — quoted three times in the New Testament. Then five woes.
chapters.3: A prayer set to music. Though the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines, yet I will rejoice in the LORD.

books.name: Zephaniah
books.scribe: Zephaniah, great-great-grandson of Hezekiah — the only prophet with royal blood in his stated genealogy.
rulers: JOSIAH, whose reforms Zephaniah likely helped provoke
books.summary: A sweeping day-of-the-LORD oracle against Judah and the nations, delivered as the young king Josiah begins tearing down the high places. It ends with God singing over his people.
prophecies: Zeph 3:17 — he will joy over thee with singing
books.captivity: None yet — Babylon is one generation away.

moves.n: I will utterly consume all things from off the land.
Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia, Assyria — and a call to the meek.
The city rebuked, then a remnant left, and God rejoicing over them with singing.

chapters.1: The great day of the LORD is near. Against those settled on their lees, who say the LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.
chapters.2: Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth. Then oracles against Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia and Assyria.
chapters.3: Woe to her that is filthy and polluted. Then an unexpected close: he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will joy over thee with singing.

books.name: Haggai
books.scribe: Haggai, one of the prophets of the return. His four messages are dated to the exact day, all within four months of 520 BC.
books.summary: The exiles came home, laid a foundation, and stopped for sixteen years. Haggai's whole message is: your houses are panelled and God's house lies waste. The work restarted within a month.
themes: The greater glory of the second house
prophecies: Hag 2:9 — the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former
books.captivity: Returned from BABYLON, rebuilding under Persian licence.

moves.n: Panelled houses, a ruined temple, and a drought nobody connected to it.
The latter glory, a lesson from priestly law, and a signet ring.

chapters.1: Is it time for you to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste? Ye have sown much, and bring in little. The people obey within a month.
chapters.2: Who is left that saw this house in her first glory? The glory of this latter house shall be greater. Zerubbabel made as a signet.

books.name: Zechariah
books.scribe: Zechariah son of Berechiah, a priest as well as a prophet, working alongside Haggai.
books.summary: Eight night visions, then oracles reaching far past the rebuilding. More quoted in the passion narratives than any prophet except Isaiah.
prophecies: Zech 4:6 — not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit
Zech 9:9 — thy King cometh… lowly, and riding upon an ass
Zech 11:12–13 — thirty pieces of silver
Zech 12:10 — they shall look upon me whom they have pierced
books.captivity: Returned.

moves.n: Horsemen, horns, a measuring line, Joshua re-robed, a lampstand, a flying roll, chariots.
A delegation asks; the answer is about justice, not calendars.
The king on a donkey, thirty pieces of silver, the pierced one, and the day of the LORD.

chapters.1: Turn ye unto me. The first two of eight night visions: the horsemen among the myrtle trees, and the four horns and four carpenters.
chapters.2: A man with a measuring line. Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls, and God himself a wall of fire round about her.
chapters.3: Joshua the high priest in filthy garments, with Satan at his right hand to resist him. The garments changed, and my servant the BRANCH promised.
chapters.4: The golden candlestick and two olive trees. Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit. Who hath despised the day of small things?
chapters.5: The flying roll, and a woman named Wickedness carried off in an ephah to Shinar.
chapters.6: Four chariots from between two mountains of brass, then crowns set on Joshua's head: behold the man whose name is The BRANCH.
chapters.7: A delegation asks whether to keep fasting. The answer is a question about whether the fasts were ever for God, and a call to execute true judgment.
chapters.8: Old men and old women shall dwell in the streets of Jerusalem, and the streets shall be full of boys and girls playing.
chapters.9: Rejoice greatly — thy King cometh unto thee, lowly, and riding upon an ass. Read at the entry into Jerusalem.
chapters.10: The LORD shall visit his flock, and make them as his goodly horse in the battle. Against shepherds who leave the sheep to wander.
chapters.11: The shepherd who breaks two staves, Beauty and Bands, and is weighed thirty pieces of silver — cast to the potter in the house of the LORD.
chapters.12: Jerusalem a cup of trembling to all the peoples. They shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and mourn as one mourneth for his only son.
chapters.13: A fountain opened for sin and for uncleanness. Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered — quoted on the night of the arrest.
chapters.14: The day of the LORD, with his feet standing upon the mount of Olives, which shall cleave in the midst. At the end, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD on the bells of the horses.

books.name: Malachi
books.scribe: Malachi — the name means 'my messenger', and some hold it is a title rather than a personal name. The last voice of the Old Testament.
books.summary: A hundred years after the return, worship has gone cynical: blemished animals on the altar, priests bored, marriages discarded, tithes withheld. Written as six disputes — God states a charge, the people answer back.
prophecies: Mal 3:1 — I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way
Mal 4:5 — I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day
laws: Tithes brought into the storehouse (3:8–10)
Divorce condemned (2:14–16)
books.captivity: Free. Then four hundred years of silence before Matthew opens.

moves.n: Blemished sacrifices, contempt for the altar, and faithless divorce.
Robbing God in tithes, the book of remembrance, and Elijah promised.

chapters.1: I have loved you, saith the LORD, and the people answer wherein? Polluted bread on the altar, and blind and lame beasts offered — offer it now unto thy governor.
chapters.2: Against the priests who caused many to stumble, and against divorce: he hateth putting away. Have we not all one father?
chapters.3: Behold, I will send my messenger. Will a man rob God? Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse. A book of remembrance written.
chapters.4: The day cometh that shall burn as an oven, but the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings. Elijah promised — the last words of the Old Testament.

books.name: 1 Esdras
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek retelling that draws on Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, probably compiled by a Jewish writer in Egypt.
books.written: c. 200–150 BC, about events from 622–458 BC
books.summary: The return from exile told again, from Josiah's passover to Ezra's reading of the law. Its one wholly original passage is the contest of the three guardsmen at Darius's court, which Zerubbabel wins by arguing that truth is stronger than wine, kings or women.
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN, ending in the Persian release.

moves.n: The passover, then four kings and the fall of Jerusalem.
Zerubbabel argues that truth is strongest, and wins the return.
Opposition, Darius's decree, and the dedication.
The scribe returns with the law and confronts mixed marriages.

chapters.1: Josiah's passover, kept with more detail than Chronicles gives, then four kings and the fall of the city in quick succession.
chapters.2: Cyrus's proclamation and the vessels returned, then the letter of complaint that halts the work under Artaxerxes.
chapters.3: The three guardsmen of Darius set a contest: which is strongest? The first says wine.
chapters.4: The second says the king; the third, Zerubbabel, says women, and then truth — and truth wins him the right to rebuild Jerusalem.
chapters.5: The register of those who went up, the altar rebuilt, and the foundation laid amid weeping and shouting mixed together.
chapters.6: Tattenai's enquiry and the search of the archives, which turns up Cyrus's original decree at Ecbatane.
chapters.7: The temple finished in the sixth year of Darius, dedicated with joy, and the passover kept.
chapters.8: Ezra comes up with the king's letter, fasts at the river Theras, and finds no Levites among those he has gathered.
chapters.9: The assembly in the rain over foreign marriages, then the reading of the law, the people weeping and being told the day is holy.

books.name: 2 Esdras
books.scribe: Unknown. A composite: the Jewish apocalypse at its core (chapters 3–14, often called 4 Ezra) was written after the fall of Jerusalem, with Christian material added at both ends.
books.written: core c. AD 90–100, additions 2nd–3rd century AD
rulers: Written under Rome, set in the reign of Artaxerxes
the eagle of the vision, read as Rome
books.summary: Seven visions given to a man who cannot accept what has happened to his city. He argues with the angel Uriel about why God permits the wicked to prosper, and is answered with an eagle, a man from the sea, and a commission to rewrite the burned scriptures.
prophecies: 2 Esd 11–12 — the eagle with twelve wings, interpreted as the empire that will be judged
books.captivity: Written in the shadow of AD 70, voiced as if in Babylon.

moves.n: Later material addressed to a rejected Israel.
Why does God allow this? The angel Uriel answers in riddles.
The mourning woman, the eagle, and the man from the sea.
Ezra dictates ninety-four books over forty days.
Oracles of judgment on the nations.

chapters.1: A Christian preface addressed to a people who have rejected their inheritance: I gathered you as a hen gathereth her chickens.
chapters.2: The kingdom offered to another nation, and a vision of a great multitude on mount Sion crowned by a young man of high stature.
chapters.3: The apocalypse proper begins in the thirtieth year after the fall of the city. Ezra's complaint: is Babylon better than Sion?
chapters.4: Uriel answers with impossible tasks — weigh me the weight of the fire, or measure me the blast of the wind.
chapters.5: Signs of the end, then the second complaint: why has one people been given up to so many?
chapters.6: The creation recalled day by day, and the answer that the age was made for Israel's sake.
chapters.7: The longest and hardest chapter: the narrow entrance, the intermediate state, and the few who are saved. It contains a long passage missing from most old manuscripts.
chapters.8: For this age is full of sadness and infirmities. Ezra pleads for mercy on the many, and is answered about the sowing of seed.
chapters.9: Signs again, then the fourth vision: a woman mourning for her only son, met in a field.
chapters.10: The woman is transfigured into a city — she is Sion, and her lost son is the sanctuary.
chapters.11: The eagle from the sea with twelve wings and three heads, understood as the fourth kingdom of Daniel's vision.
chapters.12: The lion rebukes the eagle. The interpretation is given, and Ezra is told to write it in a book and hide it.
chapters.13: A man rising out of the sea who melts a multitude with the breath of his mouth, and gathers a peaceable multitude to himself.
chapters.14: The burning bush recalled. Ezra dictates ninety-four books in forty days — twenty-four published, seventy kept for the wise.
chapters.15: A Christian appendix: oracles of judgment on Egypt, Babylon, Asia and Syria.
chapters.16: Woe to thee, Babylon. The last chapter closes with a call to be ready, for the harvest is at hand.

books.name: Tobit
books.scribe: Unknown. Written partly in the first person as Tobit's own account, then continued in the third person.
rulers: the exiles of Naphtali in Nineveh
books.summary: A domestic story set among the deported northern tribes. A blind father, a desperate young woman, a journey with a stranger who turns out to be the angel Raphael, and a marriage that undoes seven deaths.
laws: Tob 4:15 — do that to no man which thou hatest, an early form of the golden rule
books.captivity: ASSYRIAN — the ten tribes deported to Nineveh and Media.

moves.n: Tobit blinded in Nineveh; Sara accused after seven bridegrooms die.
Tobias sets out with a hired guide and a dog, and catches a fish.
Sara's demon driven off; the money recovered from Gabael.
Sight restored, the guide revealed as Raphael, and Tobit's last words.

chapters.1: Tobit's own account: deported to Nineveh, prospering under Shalmaneser, and risking everything to bury the dead the king has executed.
chapters.2: Blinded by sparrow dung while sleeping in his courtyard. His wife earns their bread and he wrongly accuses her over a goat.
chapters.3: Two prayers on the same day — Tobit's in Nineveh and Sara's in Ecbatane, after seven bridegrooms have died. Raphael is sent for both.
chapters.4: Tobit's testament to his son: give alms, honour your mother, do to no man what you hate. He mentions money left with Gabael.
chapters.5: Raphael hired as a guide under the name Azarias. The dog goes with them — one of the few dogs in scripture treated warmly.
chapters.6: A fish leaps at Tobias at the Tigris. Its heart, liver and gall are kept, and Raphael explains what each is for.
chapters.7: At Raguel's house in Ecbatane. Sara is given to Tobias, and her father quietly digs a grave that night in case.
chapters.8: The heart and liver burned on the ashes; the demon flees to Egypt. The grave is filled in before morning.
chapters.9: Raphael goes to Rages to fetch the money from Gabael while the fourteen-day wedding feast continues.
chapters.10: Tobit counts every day of the delay, and his mother sits watching the road.
chapters.11: Home again. The gall applied, the whiteness pulled away, and Tobit sees his son. Anna runs to meet them.
chapters.12: Raphael refuses payment and reveals himself: I am one of the seven holy angels. Alms doth deliver from death.
chapters.13: Tobit's psalm of thanksgiving and a prophecy of Jerusalem rebuilt with sapphire and emerald.
chapters.14: Tobit dies at a great age, having told his son to leave Nineveh because it will fall. Tobias lives to hear that it has.

books.name: Judith
books.scribe: Unknown. The history is deliberately impossible — Nebuchadnezzar is called king of the Assyrians reigning in Nineveh — which has long been read as a signal that the book is a parable rather than a chronicle.
rulers: 'Nabuchodonosor', king of the Assyrians in the book's own telling
books.summary: A besieged town has agreed to surrender in five days if God does not act. A widow walks into the enemy camp, flatters the general for three nights, and comes back with his head in a bag.
books.power: Assyria as the book names it
books.captivity: Invasion and siege, not deportation.

moves.n: Nabuchodonosor sends Holofernes west; nation after nation submits.
Bethulia's water is cut off and the town agrees to surrender in five days.
A widow rebukes the elders, prays, dresses, and walks out of the gate.
Three nights of flattery, one sword, and a rout.

chapters.1: Nabuchodonosor, called king of the Assyrians reigning at Nineveh, defeats Arphaxad and resolves to punish the west for refusing him help.
chapters.2: Holofernes sent out with a hundred and twenty thousand foot and twelve thousand archers, with orders to leave nothing alive that resists.
chapters.3: The coastal cities surrender and are garrisoned anyway, their groves cut down.
chapters.4: Judaea prepares: the passes fortified, sackcloth on the altar, and even the cattle put in sackcloth.
chapters.5: Achior the Ammonite gives Holofernes an accurate history of Israel and warns that they cannot be beaten unless they sin.
chapters.6: For this Achior is bound and left at the foot of Bethulia, where the Israelites take him in.
chapters.7: The springs seized. After thirty-four days the water fails, and the people demand surrender.
chapters.8: Judith summons the elders and rebukes them for setting God a deadline of five days.
chapters.9: Her prayer at the hour of the evening incense, recalling Simeon's vengeance for Dinah.
chapters.10: She dresses, takes her own food in a bag, and walks out through the valley. The watch is struck by her beauty and lets her through.
chapters.11: Her speech to Holofernes, calculated to the last word, promising to lead him to Jerusalem without a man of his losing his life.
chapters.12: Three days of eating only her own provisions. On the fourth he holds a banquet, meaning to have her, and drinks more than he ever had.
chapters.13: Alone with him at last, she takes his own falchion from the bedpost, prays twice, and strikes twice.
chapters.14: The head hung on the wall at daybreak. Achior faints when he sees it. The Assyrians find their general headless in his tent.
chapters.15: The camp breaks in panic and the spoil takes a month to gather. Judith is given Holofernes's tent and all his stuff.
chapters.16: Her song, echoing Miriam and Deborah. She lives to a hundred and five and never marries again.

books.name: Rest of Esther
books.scribe: Unknown — Greek additions inserted into the Hebrew Esther and later gathered at the end, which is why they are traditionally numbered 10–16. They appear here as chapters 1–7, keeping each chapter's own verse numbers.
books.summary: Six passages the Hebrew Esther does not contain: Mordecai's dream and its interpretation, the two royal decrees quoted in full, and long prayers by Mordecai and Esther. Where the Hebrew book never names God, these additions name him constantly.
books.captivity: Diaspora under Persian rule.

moves.n: Two dragons, and a little fountain that becomes a river.
Mordecai reports the eunuchs' conspiracy.
Mordecai and Esther plead before she risks the throne room.

moves.t: The audience and the second decree
moves.n: The king's anger turns; Haman's edict is revoked in full.

chapters.1: Mordecai's dream of two dragons and a little fountain that becomes a river — traditionally numbered chapter 11.
chapters.2: The plot of the two eunuchs uncovered, giving the background to the entry in the chronicles.
chapters.3: The full text of the decree against the Jews, which the Hebrew book only summarises.
chapters.4: Mordecai's prayer, insisting he refused to bow out of reverence for God and not from pride.
chapters.5: Esther's prayer, and her statement that she hates the splendour she is obliged to wear.
chapters.6: Her approach to the throne room, where the king's face is fierce, she faints, and God turns his spirit to gentleness.
chapters.7: The counter-decree quoted in full, naming Haman as a Macedonian, and the interpretation of the opening dream.

books.name: Wisdom of Solomon
books.scribe: Unknown, writing in Solomon's voice — a Greek-speaking Jew of Alexandria, thoroughly trained in Greek philosophy.
rulers: addressed to 'ye that be judges of the earth'
books.summary: An argument that righteousness outlasts death, aimed at Jews tempted to give up on their tradition. It opens with the cynics' speech about life being short so we may as well take what we can, and spends the rest of the book answering it.
prophecies: Wis 2:12–20 — the ungodly plotting against the just man, read by the early church as a passion prophecy
books.captivity: Diaspora — a Jewish minority inside a Greek city.

moves.n: The cynics' speech, and the answer that the souls of the righteous are in God's hand.
Solomon's voice: wisdom preferred before sceptres and thrones.
Adam to the Exodus retold as wisdom's work, with a long analysis of how idolatry began.

chapters.1: Love righteousness, ye that be judges of the earth. God made not death, neither hath he pleasure in the destruction of the living.
chapters.2: The speech of the ungodly: our life is short and tedious, let us crown ourselves with rosebuds. Then their plot against the just man.
chapters.3: The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God. Their hope is full of immortality; they were tried as gold in the furnace.
chapters.4: Better it is to have no children and to have virtue. Honourable age is not that which standeth in length of time.
chapters.5: The ungodly at the judgment, astonished: this was he whom we had sometimes in derision. Their hope is like thistledown.
chapters.6: Wisdom addressed to rulers, who will be judged more severely. She is easily seen of them that love her.
chapters.7: Solomon's voice: I myself also am a mortal man. Then the twenty-one epithets of wisdom, the breath of the power of God.
chapters.8: Wisdom sought as a bride. She teacheth temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude — the four cardinal virtues named outright.
chapters.9: The prayer for wisdom, closely following 1 Kings 3. For the thoughts of mortal men are miserable.
chapters.10: Wisdom traced through history from Adam to the Exodus, though no one is named — each is described rather than identified.
chapters.11: The plagues re-read: they were punished by the things wherewith they sinned. Thou lovest all the things that are.
chapters.12: Why the Canaanites were given time to repent. Thou mastering thy power judgest with equity.
chapters.13: The analysis of idolatry begins: those who study nature and do not find its maker, and the carpenter who carves a god from a leftover branch.
chapters.14: How images began — a grieving father making an image of a dead child, and a king's subjects flattering him from a distance.
chapters.15: The potter who makes both a vessel for clean uses and a god from the same clay, and knows he is doing it.
chapters.16: Egypt's plagues set against Israel's provision — quails for locusts, the brazen serpent as a sign rather than a cure.
chapters.17: The plague of darkness described from inside: a night of terror where they were prisoners of a long night, afraid of their own noises.
chapters.18: The night of the passover, and the all-powerful word leaping down from heaven. Aaron standing between the dead and the living.
chapters.19: The sea crossing, with the creation itself reordered so that the elements changed places, like notes on a psaltery.

books.name: Ecclesiasticus
books.scribe: Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem — one of the very few Old Testament-era books whose author names himself. His GRANDSON translated it into Greek in Egypt and wrote the prologue explaining the difficulty of the job.
books.written: written c. 180 BC, translated c. 132 BC
rulers: Simon the high priest, praised in chapter 50
books.summary: The longest book of the Apocrypha and the closest in spirit to Proverbs. A working sage's advice on money, friendship, doctors, table manners, women, slaves and death, closing with a roll call of Israel's famous men.
laws: Sir 38:1 — honour a physician, the earliest Jewish endorsement of medicine as a calling
books.power: Greek rule from Egypt and Syria
books.captivity: Free, but under Hellenistic pressure.

moves.t: The grandson's preface and first counsels
moves.n: On translation, the fear of the Lord, patience and friendship.
Money, speech, women, servants, doctors, dreams, table manners.
Wisdom describes herself as taking root in Jacob.
Old age, children, almsgiving, and a hymn on the works of creation.

moves.t: Let us now praise famous men
moves.n: Enoch to Simon the high priest, in sequence.
A personal thanksgiving and an appeal to the unlearned.

chapters.1: All wisdom cometh from the Lord. The fear of the Lord is the beginning, the fulness and the crown of wisdom.
chapters.2: My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation. Gold is tried in the fire.
chapters.3: Honour thy father in word and deed. The greater thou art, the more humble thyself. Water quencheth a flaming fire, and alms maketh atonement.
chapters.4: Defend the fatherless. Wisdom exalteth her children; she walketh with him at the first by crooked ways, then bringeth him the straight way.
chapters.5: Set not thy heart upon thy goods. Be not confident of forgiveness, to add sin unto sin.
chapters.6: A faithful friend is a strong defence, and the medicine of life. Come unto her with thy whole heart.
chapters.7: Do no evil, so shall no harm come unto thee. Forget not thy friend in thy mind, and be not unmindful of him in thy riches.
chapters.8: Strive not with a mighty man, nor with a rich man, nor with one that is full of tongue. Miss not the discourse of the elders.
chapters.9: Warnings about women, and about the company one keeps. Forsake not an old friend, for the new is not comparable to him.
chapters.10: A wise judge will instruct his people. Pride is hateful before God and man. Why is earth and ashes proud?
chapters.11: Judge none blessed before his death. Many kings have sat down upon the ground, and one that was never thought of hath worn the crown.
chapters.12: On giving and on false friends. If thou be for his profit, he will use thee; if thou have nothing, he will forsake thee.
chapters.13: He that toucheth pitch shall be defiled. What agreement is there between the hyena and a dog, or the rich and the poor?
chapters.14: The miser who is evil to himself, and the blessedness of the man who dies before he grows weary of living.
chapters.15: He hath set fire and water before thee: stretch forth thine hand unto whether thou wilt. Say not thou, It is through the Lord that I fell away.
chapters.16: Desire not a multitude of unprofitable children. His mercy is great, and he forgiveth and repenteth — but his wrath is upon sinners.
chapters.17: The Lord created man of the earth, and gave him a tongue, eyes and ears. Return unto the Lord, and forsake thy sins.
chapters.18: What is man, and whereto serveth he? A man's days at the most are a hundred years — as a drop of water unto the sea.
chapters.19: He that contemneth small things shall fall by little and little. Admonish a friend, it may be he hath not done it.
chapters.20: There is a rebuke that is not comely, and there is a man that holdeth his tongue and is found wise. A lie is a foul blot in a man.
chapters.21: The foolish man's talk is like a burden in the way, but grace shall be found in the lips of the wise.
chapters.22: The slothful man is compared to a filthy stone. A friendship may be reconciled after wounding — but not after upbraiding.
chapters.23: A prayer against the tongue and against desire. Accustom not thy mouth to swearing.
chapters.24: Wisdom praises herself in the congregation. She took root in an honourable people, and is identified with the book of the covenant.
chapters.25: Nine things esteemed happy. The fear of the Lord passeth all. Give me any plague, but the plague of the heart.
chapters.26: A virtuous woman rejoiceth her husband. Two things grieve the writer's heart, and a third maketh him angry.
chapters.27: He that casteth a stone on high casteth it on his own head. Whoso discovereth secrets loseth his credit.
chapters.28: He that revengeth shall find vengeance. Forgive thy neighbour the hurt he hath done. The tongue has cast out virtuous women.
chapters.29: Lend to thy neighbour in time of his need. Better is the life of a poor man in a mean cottage than delicate fare in another man's house.
chapters.30: He that loveth his son causeth him oft to feel the rod. Gladness of the heart is the life of man, and the joyfulness of a man prolongeth his days.
chapters.31: Watching for riches consumeth the flesh. Wine measured out is as good as life; drunkenness increaseth the rage of a fool.
chapters.32: Advice for a master of a feast: speak briefly, and hinder not musick. Do nothing without advice, and when thou hast once done, repent not.
chapters.33: As clay in the potter's hand, so is man in the hand of him that made him. Advice on servants, given plainly and hard.
chapters.34: The hopes of a man void of understanding are vain. He that washeth himself after touching a dead body, what availeth his washing?
chapters.35: He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough. The prayer of the humble pierceth the clouds.
chapters.36: A prayer for the whole nation: have mercy upon us, O Lord, and gather all the tribes of Jacob together.
chapters.37: Every counsellor extolleth counsel, but there is some that counselleth for himself. A man's mind is sometime wont to tell him more than seven watchmen.
chapters.38: Honour a physician with the honour due unto him, for the Lord hath created him — the earliest Jewish endorsement of medicine as a calling. Then on mourning, and on the crafts.
chapters.39: The scribe who gives his mind to the law of the most High, and rises early to pray. All the works of the Lord are good.
chapters.40: Great travail is created for every man. There is no want in the fear of the Lord. Better is death than a bitter life.
chapters.41: O death, how bitter is the remembrance of thee to a man that liveth at rest. Then a list of the things one should be ashamed of.
chapters.42: Be not ashamed of the law of the most High. The works of the Lord in creation, who hath measured them all.
chapters.43: The pride of the height, the sun, the moon, the rainbow, snow and frost. We may speak much, and yet come short: he is all.
chapters.44: Let us now praise famous men. Some there be which have no memorial; but these were merciful men, whose righteousness hath not been forgotten.
chapters.45: Moses, Aaron and Phinehas, with Aaron's vestments described in loving detail.
chapters.46: Joshua and Caleb, the judges, and Samuel, who called upon the Lord when his enemies pressed him on every side.
chapters.47: Nathan, David and Solomon — and a blunt account of how Solomon stained his honour and bowed his loins to women.
chapters.48: Elijah and Elisha, then Hezekiah and Isaiah, who saw by an excellent spirit what should come to pass at the last.
chapters.49: Josiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the twelve prophets, then Zerubbabel, Joshua and Nehemiah.
chapters.50: Simon the high priest coming out from behind the veil, described like sunrise, like the moon at the full, like the rainbow.
chapters.51: A closing prayer and a personal account of seeking wisdom from youth. Put your neck under the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction.

books.name: Baruch
books.scribe: Attributed to Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe. Chapter 6 is a separate work, the Epistle of Jeremy, attached to it.
books.summary: A confession read aloud to the exiles by the river, followed by a poem on wisdom and a promise that Jerusalem will see her children come home. The appended letter is a sustained mockery of idols that cannot save themselves from rust.
themes: Wisdom found only in the law
prophecies: Bar 4:36–37 — look about thee toward the east, and behold thy children gathered from the west
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — written to and for the deported.

moves.n: Read aloud by the river, admitting the exile is deserved.
Wisdom is found in the book of the commandments; Jerusalem speaks to her children.
Put off the garment of mourning; God will level the mountains for the road home.
A separate letter ridiculing idols that cannot dust themselves.

chapters.1: The book read aloud by the river Sud to Jechonias and the exiles, who send money and the letter back to Jerusalem.
chapters.2: The confession continues: we have not hearkened. The dead in the grave shall not give unto the Lord praise; the soul that is greatly vexed shall give thee praise.
chapters.3: O Israel, why art thou in thine enemies' land? The poem on wisdom — the giants perished for want of it, and no one has found the way to her but God.
chapters.4: Wisdom identified with the book of the commandments of God. Then Jerusalem speaks to her children and is answered: be of good cheer.
chapters.5: Put off, O Jerusalem, the garment of thy mourning. God has commanded that the high mountains be made low, that Israel may go safely.
chapters.6: The Epistle of Jeremy, a separate work: a long, dry demolition of idols, who cannot save themselves from rust, moths, or a fire in their own temple.

books.name: Song of the Three Children
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek addition placed inside Daniel 3, between verses 23 and 24.
books.summary: What the three men said inside the furnace. Azarias prays a confession for the whole nation, then all three sing a long call to every created thing — sun, frost, whales, fowls — to bless the Lord.
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — set inside the fiery furnace.

moves.n: Azarias's confession, the angel driving out the flame, and the song of all creation.

chapters.1: The prayer of Azarias inside the furnace, confessing for the whole nation, then the angel driving out the flame, and the song calling every created thing to bless the Lord.

books.name: Susanna
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek addition to Daniel, placed before chapter 1 in some manuscripts and after chapter 12 in others.
books.summary: Two respected judges corner a woman in her garden and threaten to ruin her if she refuses them. She refuses, they perjure her to a death sentence, and a young Daniel stops the execution by cross-examining them separately about which tree they saw her under.
laws: The law on false witnesses — Deut 19:18–19 applied to the elders in the closing verses
books.captivity: BABYLONIAN — the exiled community governing itself.

moves.n: Two elders, a false charge, a death sentence, and Daniel's cross-examination.

chapters.1: Two elders appointed judges corner Susanna in her garden. She refuses, they perjure her to a death sentence, and a young Daniel stops the execution by asking each separately which tree he saw her under.

books.name: Bel and the Dragon
books.scribe: Unknown — a Greek addition to Daniel, told as two detective stories.
books.summary: Daniel proves the idol Bel does not eat its offerings by scattering ashes on the temple floor overnight and showing the king the priests' footprints. He then kills a living dragon with a cake of pitch, fat and hair, and survives a second stay among lions.
books.captivity: Post-exilic, at the Persian court.

moves.t: Bel, the dragon, and the lions
moves.n: Ashes on the floor, a cake of pitch, and a second den.

chapters.1: Daniel proves Bel does not eat by scattering ashes and showing the king the priests' footprints, then kills a living dragon with a cake of pitch, fat and hair, and survives a second den of lions.

books.name: Prayer of Manasses
books.scribe: Unknown, written in the voice of King Manasseh of Judah. 2 Chr 33:18–19 refers to a prayer of Manasseh in the records of the kings; this is an attempt to supply it.
rulers: the Assyrian king who took him in chains to Babylon
books.summary: Fifteen verses of penitence from the worst king Judah ever had, written after his captivity broke him. One of the most concentrated confessions in scripture — it never asks for anything but pardon.
books.captivity: Manasseh himself taken with hooks to Babylon (2 Chr 33:11) and later restored.

moves.n: Fifteen verses of confession from a king who had filled Jerusalem with idols.

chapters.1: Fifteen verses of penitence in the voice of Judah's worst king, written to supply the prayer 2 Chronicles only mentions. It asks for nothing but pardon.

books.name: 1 Maccabees
books.scribe: Unknown — a Jewish historian writing in Hebrew, sober and closely dated. Widely regarded as the most reliable history in the Apocrypha, and Josephus leans on it heavily.
books.written: c. 100 BC, about events from 175–134 BC
books.summary: The revolt that fills the silence between the Testaments. A Seleucid king outlaws the Jewish religion and puts an idol in the Temple; a village priest refuses to sacrifice, and his five sons fight a guerrilla war that ends in an independent Jewish state.
laws: 1 Macc 2:41 — the ruling that Jews may fight in self-defence on the sabbath, after a thousand died refusing to
books.captivity: OCCUPATION AND FORCED HELLENIZATION — the Temple desecrated in 167 BC, rededicated in 164.

moves.n: Antiochus loots the Temple; Mattathias refuses to sacrifice and starts the revolt.
Victories against long odds, the Temple cleansed, and Judas's death in battle.
Diplomacy with rival Seleucid claimants; treaties with Rome and Sparta.
Tribute lifted, the citadel taken, and a hereditary priest-rulership established.

chapters.1: Alexander's empire divided, then Antiochus Epiphanes looting the temple and outlawing the religion. The abomination of desolation set on the altar.
chapters.2: Mattathias refuses to sacrifice at Modin and kills the man who does. The ruling that Jews may fight on the sabbath, after a thousand died refusing to.
chapters.3: Judas Maccabeus takes command and beats Apollonius and Seron. Lysias is sent against him with a great army.
chapters.4: Victory at Emmaus and Bethsura, then the temple cleansed and rededicated, and the eight-day feast established — the origin of Hanukkah.
chapters.5: Campaigns in Galilee and Gilead to bring endangered Jewish communities home.
chapters.6: Antiochus dies in Persia. His son comes with elephants, and Eleazar is crushed under the one he stabs from beneath.
chapters.7: Alcimus and Bacchides, then Nicanor, who threatens the temple and is defeated at Adasa.
chapters.8: The treaty with Rome, whose power is described admiringly and at length by a writer who has not yet seen what it costs.
chapters.9: Judas falls at Elasa against overwhelming odds. Jonathan takes his place and fights on from the wilderness.
chapters.10: Rival Seleucid claimants bid for Jonathan's support. He is made high priest and clothed in purple.
chapters.11: The politics grow tangled — Ptolemy, Demetrius, Trypho — with Jonathan playing each against the others.
chapters.12: Letters to Sparta and Rome renewing friendship. Trypho takes Jonathan by treachery at Ptolemais.
chapters.13: Simon succeeds, buries his brother at Modin under a monument of seven pyramids, and secures the removal of tribute.
chapters.14: A time of peace: they made the land quiet, and every man sat under his vine and his fig tree. Simon confirmed as leader and high priest for ever.
chapters.15: Antiochus VII first courts Simon, then demands the cities back and sends an army.
chapters.16: Simon and two of his sons murdered at a banquet by his own son-in-law. John Hyrcanus succeeds — and the book stops.

books.name: 2 Maccabees
books.scribe: An unnamed epitomist, who says outright that he has condensed five books by Jason of Cyrene into one and found the work exhausting.
books.written: c. 124–100 BC, about events from 180–161 BC
rulers: Onias III, the murdered high priest
books.summary: Not a sequel but a parallel account, covering a shorter span with more theology and more horror. It contains the martyrdom of Eleazar and of the mother with seven sons, and the clearest Old Testament-era statement of bodily resurrection.
prophecies: 2 Macc 7:9, 14 — the King of the world shall raise us up unto everlasting life
books.captivity: OCCUPATION — the persecution under Antiochus IV, told from the martyrs' side.

moves.n: Two letters to Egypt, and the epitomist explaining his method.
Heliodorus stopped in the treasury; the high priesthood sold and resold.
Eleazar refuses to fake eating; a mother watches seven sons die.
The revolt gathers, Antiochus dies, the Temple is purified.
Lysias, Nicanor, and the institution of a commemorative day.

chapters.1: Two letters to the Jews of Egypt urging them to keep the feast, with the story of the hidden fire that became thick water.
chapters.2: Jeremiah hiding the tabernacle, the ark and the altar in a cave. Then the epitomist explains he is condensing five books of Jason of Cyrene, and says it is hard work.
chapters.3: Heliodorus comes for the treasury and is struck down by a rider and two young men, then healed at the high priest's prayer.
chapters.4: The high priesthood bought and sold — Jason, then Menelaus — and the murder of the deposed Onias.
chapters.5: Visions of horsemen over Jerusalem, then Antiochus sacking the city and Apollonius killing on the sabbath.
chapters.6: The temple rededicated to Olympian Jupiter. Eleazar, ninety years old, refuses even to pretend to eat swine's flesh.
chapters.7: The mother and her seven sons, tortured one by one. The clearest statement of bodily resurrection in the Old Testament era.
chapters.8: Judas gathers six thousand and begins winning. Nicanor, who had sold Jews in advance to pay Rome, flees in disguise.
chapters.9: Antiochus dies of a foul disease, writing a letter of promises no one believes.
chapters.10: The temple purified and the feast kept for eight days. Then campaigns against Idumea and Timotheus.
chapters.11: Lysias defeated at Bethsura, and four letters quoted granting terms to the Jews.
chapters.12: After a battle, idols are found under the dead. Judas sends money to Jerusalem for a sin offering for them — the passage later cited in arguments about prayers for the dead.
chapters.13: Menelaus executed by being thrown from a tower of ashes. Antiochus V makes peace and departs.
chapters.14: Nicanor returns and at first befriends Judas. Razis, an elder of Jerusalem, kills himself rather than be taken.
chapters.15: Judas's dream of Onias and Jeremiah, then Nicanor's defeat and death, and a day appointed to remember it. The epitomist signs off apologising for his style.

books.name: Matthew
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint Matthew
books.scribe: Matthew, also called Levi, a tax collector called from his booth — a man trained to keep records, writing for a Jewish readership.
books.summary: The Gospel that keeps pointing backwards — over sixty quotations from the prophets, and a genealogy that opens the New Testament by tying Jesus to Abraham and David. Built around five great blocks of teaching.
prophecies: Mt 24 — the Olivet discourse: the Temple's destruction, fulfilled in AD 70
laws: The Sermon on the Mount (5–7) — the Law intensified, not repealed
Mt 22:37–40 — the two commandments on which hang all the law and the prophets
books.captivity: Occupation — a client kingdom under Roman prefects.

moves.n: Genealogy, virgin birth, magi, flight to Egypt, baptism, temptation.
The first teaching block: the constitution of the kingdom.
Miracles in series, then the twelve sent out.
Rejection hardens; teaching shifts into parables.
Peter's confession, the transfiguration, and instructions on community.
The triumphal entry, seven woes, and the Olivet discourse.
Arrest, trial, crucifixion, resurrection, go ye therefore.

chapters.1: The genealogy in three sets of fourteen, running through Abraham and David. Four women appear in it, each with an irregular story. Then the angel's word to Joseph.
chapters.2: Wise men from the east, Herod's enquiry of the scribes, and the flight into Egypt. The slaughter at Bethlehem, and Rachel weeping again.
chapters.3: John the Baptist in the wilderness, preaching repentance and refusing the Pharisees. The baptism, the opened heaven, and the voice.
chapters.4: Forty days in the wilderness and three temptations, each answered from Deuteronomy. The ministry begins in Galilee; the first four disciples are called from their nets.
chapters.5: The Sermon on the Mount opens with the Beatitudes, then salt and light, then the six antitheses — ye have heard it said, but I say unto you.
chapters.6: Almsgiving, prayer and fasting done in secret. The Lord's Prayer sits in the middle. No man can serve two masters; consider the lilies.
chapters.7: Judge not; ask and it shall be given; the narrow gate; false prophets known by fruits. Ends with two houses, one on rock and one on sand.
chapters.8: Nine miracles begin: a leper touched, a centurion's servant healed at a distance, a storm stilled, and the demoniacs at Gadara.
chapters.9: Matthew called from the receipt of custom. The paralytic forgiven before he is healed, and the question about fasting answered with new wine and old bottles.
chapters.10: The twelve are named and sent out with instructions: no scrip, no two coats. Warnings of division, and not a sparrow falls without your Father.
chapters.11: John sends from prison to ask whether Jesus is the one. Woes on Chorazin and Bethsaida, then the invitation: come unto me, all ye that labour.
chapters.12: Sabbath controversies over corn and a withered hand. The unforgivable sin, and the sign of Jonah promised to a generation asking for a sign.
chapters.13: Seven parables of the kingdom: sower, tares, mustard seed, leaven, treasure, pearl, and net. He speaks to the crowds only in parables.
chapters.14: John the Baptist beheaded at a birthday feast. Five thousand fed with five loaves, and Peter walks on water until he sees the wind.
chapters.15: Tradition versus commandment — defilement comes out of the mouth, not into it. The Canaanite woman's answer about crumbs from the master's table.
chapters.16: Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, and the first prediction of the passion. Peter objects and is called Satan within six verses of being called blessed.
chapters.17: The transfiguration, with Moses and Elijah. Coming down, a boy is healed whom the disciples could not help; the tribute money is found in a fish.
chapters.18: Greatness measured by a child. The lost sheep, the process for a brother who sins, and the servant forgiven ten thousand talents who will not forgive a hundred pence.
chapters.19: Divorce questioned and answered from Genesis. Children blessed, and the rich young ruler who goes away sorrowful.
chapters.20: Labourers hired at different hours and paid the same. The mother of James and John asks for thrones; the answer is a cup and a ransom.
chapters.21: The entry on a colt, the cleansing of the Temple, the fig tree cursed, and the parable of the wicked husbandmen aimed squarely at the chief priests.
chapters.22: The wedding feast, then four questions in succession: tribute to Caesar, the resurrection, the great commandment, and David's son.
chapters.23: Seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees — whited sepulchres, straining at a gnat. Ends in lament over Jerusalem, a hen and her chickens.
chapters.24: The Olivet discourse. Not one stone left upon another; wars and rumours of wars; the abomination of desolation; no man knows the day nor the hour.
chapters.25: Three parables of readiness: ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats separated on what was done to the least of these.
chapters.26: The anointing at Bethany, the Last Supper, Gethsemane, the arrest, the trial before Caiaphas, and Peter's three denials before the cock crows.
chapters.27: Judas hangs himself. Pilate washes his hands, Barabbas is released, and the crucifixion is narrated plainly. The veil is rent and the tombs opened.
chapters.28: The earthquake and the empty tomb. The guards bribed to say the body was stolen, and the Great Commission given on a mountain in Galilee.

books.name: Mark
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint Mark
books.scribe: John Mark, companion of Peter and of Paul. Early tradition (Papias, c. AD 130) says he wrote down Peter's preaching — which explains the eyewitness detail and the unflattering portrait of Peter.
rulers: possibly Nero at the time of writing
books.summary: The shortest and fastest Gospel — 'straightway' appears more than forty times. Written for Romans: Aramaic phrases are translated, Jewish customs explained, and the action starts with no genealogy at all.
prophecies: Mk 13 — not one stone shall be left upon another
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: Straightway — healings, storms, feedings, and growing crowds.
Peter's confession, three passion predictions, the road to Jerusalem.
The entry, the cleansed temple, the withered fig tree, the last days.
Gethsemane, trial, crucifixion — and an ending that stops abruptly.

chapters.1: No genealogy and no nativity — straight to John, the baptism, and the wilderness in two verses. Then a day in Capernaum, told at a run.
chapters.2: A paralytic lowered through the roof. Levi called, questions about fasting, and the sabbath made for man.
chapters.3: The withered hand healed and the plot begun. The twelve appointed; his friends say he is beside himself, and his family come to fetch him.
chapters.4: The sower, the lamp, the seed growing secretly, and the mustard seed. Then the storm stilled, and the question: how is it that ye have no faith?
chapters.5: The Gadarene demoniac and the swine, then two intertwined healings — Jairus's daughter, and the woman who touched his garment in the crowd.
chapters.6: Rejected at Nazareth, where he could do no mighty work. The twelve sent out, John beheaded, the five thousand fed, and the walking on the sea.
chapters.7: Tradition and defilement, the Syrophenician woman, and the deaf man healed with fingers, spittle and the word Ephphatha.
chapters.8: The four thousand fed, a blind man healed in two stages, Peter's confession, and the first passion prediction with its rebuke.
chapters.9: The transfiguration, the boy with the dumb spirit and his father's cry — Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. Then arguments about who is greatest.
chapters.10: Divorce, children, the rich man, the third passion prediction, James and John's request, and blind Bartimaeus who will not be quieted.
chapters.11: The entry, the fig tree cursed and found withered, the Temple cleansed, and the question about John's authority turned back on the questioners.
chapters.12: The wicked husbandmen, tribute to Caesar, the resurrection, the great commandment, and the widow's two mites weighed against the treasury.
chapters.13: The little apocalypse, delivered privately to four disciples opposite the Temple. Watch is the repeated command.
chapters.14: The anointing, the Passover, Gethsemane, the arrest, the young man who flees naked, the trial, and Peter's denial.
chapters.15: Pilate, Barabbas, the mocking, Simon of Cyrene, and the crucifixion at the third hour. The centurion's confession at the moment of death.
chapters.16: The women at the tomb ask who will roll away the stone. The oldest manuscripts end at verse 8, with the women afraid; the remaining verses are a later ending.

books.name: Luke
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint Luke
books.scribe: Luke, a physician and Paul's travelling companion — the only Gentile author in the Bible. He opens by saying he investigated everything from the first and interviewed eyewitnesses.
rulers: Caesar Augustus, whose census opens the book
books.summary: The most historically anchored Gospel, dating events by emperors and governors. It gives the most attention to women, the poor, Samaritans and outsiders, and holds the parables of the good Samaritan and the prodigal son.
prophecies: Lk 21:24 — Jerusalem trodden down of the Gentiles
books.captivity: Occupation.

moves.n: John and Jesus, with four songs; dated by emperor and governor.
Baptism, genealogy back to Adam, the Nazareth sermon, the twelve.
Ten chapters on the road: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus.
The entry, the temple, the widow's mites, the coming judgment.
The supper, the trial, the cross, and a seven-mile walk with a stranger.

chapters.1: A formal preface addressed to Theophilus, then two annunciations — to Zacharias in the Temple and to Mary at Nazareth. The Magnificat and the Benedictus.
chapters.2: The census, the manger, and shepherds. Then the presentation, Simeon and Anna, and the boy of twelve left behind in the Temple.
chapters.3: John's preaching, with practical answers for soldiers and publicans. The genealogy runs backwards, past Abraham, to Adam and to God.
chapters.4: The temptations, then Nazareth: he reads Isaiah 61, stops mid-sentence, and says it is fulfilled today. They try to throw him off a cliff.
chapters.5: The catch of fish and Peter's 'depart from me'. A leper cleansed, the paralytic through the tiles, and Levi's feast for his colleagues.
chapters.6: Sabbath disputes, the twelve chosen, then the Sermon on the Plain — blessings with matching woes, and love your enemies.
chapters.7: The centurion's servant, the widow's son at Nain, John's question from prison, and the woman who washes his feet in a Pharisee's house.
chapters.8: The women who supported the ministry named. The sower, the storm, the Gadarene, and Jairus's daughter with the interruption on the way.
chapters.9: The twelve sent out, the five thousand, Peter's confession, the transfiguration, and the turn: he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem.
chapters.10: Seventy sent out two by two. The good Samaritan answers 'who is my neighbour', and Martha is answered about Mary.
chapters.11: The Lord's Prayer given on request, the friend at midnight, the strong man armed, and woes on Pharisees and lawyers over dinner.
chapters.12: The rich fool who builds bigger barns. Do not be anxious; sell what you have; be like servants waiting for their lord to return.
chapters.13: The tower of Siloam, the barren fig tree given one more year, the woman bowed for eighteen years, and the lament over Jerusalem.
chapters.14: A sabbath dinner: choosing the lowest room, inviting those who cannot repay, the great supper with its excuses, and counting the cost.
chapters.15: Three parables for grumbling Pharisees — the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the son who was lost, with the elder brother left outside at the end.
chapters.16: The unjust steward commended for shrewdness, and the rich man and Lazarus, where the gulf is fixed and Moses and the prophets are enough.
chapters.17: Ten lepers healed and one Samaritan returns. The kingdom comes not with observation; remember Lot's wife.
chapters.18: The importunate widow and the unjust judge, the Pharisee and the publican, the children, the rich ruler, and blind Bartimaeus at Jericho.
chapters.19: Zacchaeus up a sycamore tree and down again. The pounds, the entry with the stones that would cry out, and weeping over the city.
chapters.20: The authority question, the vineyard, tribute to Caesar, the Sadducees on resurrection, and a warning about scribes who devour widows' houses.
chapters.21: The widow's mites, the destruction foretold, and Jerusalem compassed with armies — Luke's version is noticeably more concrete than Mark's.
chapters.22: The Passover and the new covenant in his blood. The dispute about greatness at the table itself, Gethsemane, the arrest, and Peter's denial — with a look.
chapters.23: Sent to Herod and back. Barabbas, Simon of Cyrene, the daughters of Jerusalem, and the penitent thief promised paradise today.
chapters.24: The empty tomb, then the road to Emmaus where he expounds the scriptures unrecognised and is known in the breaking of bread. The ascension at Bethany.

books.name: John
books.full: The Gospel According to Saint John
books.scribe: John the apostle, son of Zebedee — who refers to himself only as the disciple whom Jesus loved. Written last, decades after the others.
rulers: Domitian at the time of writing
Pilate and Caiaphas in the narrative
books.summary: Ninety per cent of its material is found in no other Gospel. Built around seven signs and seven 'I am' sayings, and it states its purpose outright in 20:31 — these are written that ye might believe.
prophecies: Jn 14:16 — another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever
laws: Jn 13:34 — a new commandment: that ye love one another
books.captivity: Occupation; the Temple already destroyed by the time of writing.

moves.n: In the beginning was the Word — the Gospel's thesis in eighteen verses.
Seven signs from Cana to Lazarus, each followed by argument.
The basin and towel, the vine, the Comforter, and the high priestly prayer.
Trial before Pilate, the cross, the garden, Thomas, and breakfast on the shore.

chapters.1: The prologue: in the beginning was the Word. Then John's testimony, the Lamb of God, and the first disciples — come and see.
chapters.2: Water into wine at Cana, the first sign, done at a wedding at his mother's prompting. Then the Temple cleansed with a scourge of small cords.
chapters.3: Nicodemus by night and the new birth. The serpent lifted in the wilderness, and the verse that follows it. John's last testimony: he must increase.
chapters.4: The Samaritan woman at Jacob's well at noon, the longest conversation he has with anyone in this Gospel. Then a nobleman's son healed from a distance.
chapters.5: The pool of Bethesda and a man ill thirty-eight years, healed on the sabbath. The discourse that follows claims equality with the Father.
chapters.6: The five thousand, the walking on the sea, and the bread of life discourse in the synagogue at Capernaum, after which many disciples go back.
chapters.7: The feast of tabernacles. The officers return without him, saying never man spake like this man. Nicodemus raises a point of law.
chapters.8: The woman taken in adultery (absent from the earliest manuscripts), the light of the world, and the confrontation ending in before Abraham was, I am.
chapters.9: The man born blind, healed with clay and Siloam. The interrogation is the real subject; his parents will not answer, and he ends up cast out.
chapters.10: The good shepherd who lays down his life, and the sheep who know the voice. At the feast of dedication they take up stones again.
chapters.11: Lazarus. Jesus waits two days, weeps at the grave, and calls him out. From that day the council takes counsel to put him to death.
chapters.12: Mary anoints his feet with spikenard. The entry into Jerusalem, Greeks asking to see him, and the corn of wheat that must fall into the ground.
chapters.13: The feet washed at supper, the new commandment, the sop given to Judas, and the prediction of Peter's denial.
chapters.14: Let not your heart be troubled. The way, the truth and the life; the promise of the Comforter; peace I leave with you.
chapters.15: The vine and the branches. Abide in me. Greater love hath no man than this; and a warning that the world will hate them.
chapters.16: The work of the Comforter explained. Sorrow turned to joy like a woman in travail. In the world ye shall have tribulation.
chapters.17: The high priestly prayer — for himself, for the disciples, and for those who will believe through their word. That they all may be one.
chapters.18: Gethsemane and the arrest, Peter's sword and Malchus's ear. Before Annas and Caiaphas, then Pilate: what is truth?
chapters.19: The scourging, the crown of thorns, Behold the man. The crucifixion, his mother given to the disciple, It is finished, and the spear thrust.
chapters.20: Mary Magdalene at the tomb, the race of Peter and John, the appearance behind locked doors, and Thomas eight days later.
chapters.21: The lakeside epilogue: the catch of a hundred and fifty three fish, breakfast on the shore, and Peter asked three times whether he loves him.

books.name: Acts
books.scribe: Luke, writing volume two to the same man, Theophilus. From chapter 16 the narrative shifts to 'we' — the author has joined the journey.
books.summary: Thirty years in which a movement of a hundred and twenty people in one room reaches the capital of the empire. Structured by Jesus's own line in 1:8 — Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, the uttermost part of the earth.
prophecies: Acts 1:8 — the programme statement, fulfilled by the last chapter
Acts 2:16–21 — Peter reads Pentecost as Joel's prophecy fulfilled
laws: Acts 15 — the Jerusalem council rules that Gentile believers are not bound to the Mosaic law
books.captivity: Paul ends the book under house arrest in Rome, preaching without hindrance.

moves.n: Ascension, Pentecost, the first church, Stephen's death.
Philip, Saul's conversion, Cornelius, Antioch, Peter's escape.
Cyprus and Galatia with Barnabas.
The question of Gentile circumcision settled at Jerusalem.
Philippi, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus — and the 'we' passages begin.
Riot, five trials, appeal to Caesar, shipwreck, and two years in a hired house.

chapters.1: Forty days of appearances, then the ascension and the question about restoring the kingdom, left unanswered. Matthias chosen by lot to replace Judas.
chapters.2: Pentecost: wind, tongues of fire, and every man hearing in his own language. Peter preaches from Joel and Psalms; three thousand are added.
chapters.3: The lame man at the Beautiful gate — silver and gold have I none. The healing draws a crowd and Peter preaches in Solomon's porch.
chapters.4: Peter and John before the council, which notes they are unlearned men. The believers hold all things common.
chapters.5: Ananias and Sapphira drop dead over a withheld price. The apostles are jailed and freed by night; Gamaliel counsels leaving them alone.
chapters.6: Greek-speaking widows overlooked in the daily distribution. Seven are appointed to serve tables, Stephen among them.
chapters.7: Stephen's defence retells the whole national story from Abraham to Solomon, then turns on his judges. He is stoned; Saul holds the coats.
chapters.8: Persecution scatters the church. Philip in Samaria, Simon who offers money for the gift, and the Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah in his chariot.
chapters.9: The road to Damascus, the blindness, and Ananias sent to a man he has every reason to fear. Then Aeneas healed and Dorcas raised.
chapters.10: Cornelius the centurion, and Peter's rooftop vision of the sheet — what God hath cleansed, call not thou common. The Spirit falls on Gentiles.
chapters.11: Peter has to explain himself in Jerusalem. The gospel reaches Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians.
chapters.12: James is killed with the sword. Peter is freed by an angel and Rhoda leaves him standing at the gate. Herod is struck down for taking glory.
chapters.13: Barnabas and Saul sent from Antioch. Cyprus, Elymas struck blind, and the sermon at Antioch in Pisidia that ends with a turn to the Gentiles.
chapters.14: At Lystra they are taken for Jupiter and Mercurius, then Paul is stoned and left for dead. They return by the same towns confirming the disciples.
chapters.15: The Jerusalem council on whether Gentiles must be circumcised. James proposes the four abstentions. Paul and Barnabas part over Mark.
chapters.16: Timothy joins. The Macedonian vision, Lydia the seller of purple, and the earthquake that opens the Philippian jail at midnight.
chapters.17: Thessalonica and Berea, where they search the scriptures daily. Then Athens, the altar to the unknown God, and the speech on Mars' hill.
chapters.18: Corinth, Aquila and Priscilla, and eighteen months of tentmaking and teaching. Gallio refuses to hear the case. Apollos is instructed more perfectly.
chapters.19: Ephesus: handkerchiefs carried from Paul's body, the sons of Sceva overpowered, books of magic burned, and a riot led by the silversmiths.
chapters.20: Eutychus falls from a third-loft window during a long sermon. The farewell at Miletus — it is more blessed to give than to receive.
chapters.21: Agabus binds his own hands with Paul's girdle. Paul goes to Jerusalem anyway and is seized in the Temple on a false report.
chapters.22: Paul addresses the crowd in Hebrew. The word Gentiles ends the hearing. He stops a scourging by asking whether it is lawful to whip a Roman.
chapters.23: Before the council he sets Pharisees against Sadducees over the resurrection. Forty men vow to kill him; his nephew reports the plot.
chapters.24: Before Felix at Caesarea, with Tertullus prosecuting. Felix trembles at the reasoning, hopes for a bribe, and leaves Paul bound for two years.
chapters.25: Festus inherits the case. Paul appeals unto Caesar, which settles where he will be tried and how he will reach Rome.
chapters.26: Before Agrippa: the conversion told a third time. Festus calls him mad; Agrippa says almost thou persuadest me.
chapters.27: The voyage and the shipwreck, told with a sailor's detail — soundings, undergirding the ship, cutting away the boat. All 276 come safe to land.
chapters.28: The viper on Malta that does no harm. Rome at last, two years in his own hired house, preaching with no man forbidding him. The book simply stops.

books.name: Romans
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Romans
books.scribe: Paul, dictated to TERTIUS, who inserts his own greeting in 16:22 — one of the few named scribes in scripture.
books.summary: Paul's most systematic letter, written to a church he had not yet visited, laying out sin, justification by faith, the Spirit, the place of Israel, and what all of it means on a Tuesday.
prophecies: Rom 11:25–26 — blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles
laws: Rom 13:1–7 — the believer's obligation to civil authority
Rom 13:10 — love is the fulfilling of the law
books.captivity: None — written in freedom, before the imprisonments.

moves.n: All have sinned — Gentile, Jew and moralist alike.
Abraham as the test case; peace with God.
Dead to sin, free from law, alive in the Spirit — and nothing can separate.
Election, the olive tree, and a hardening that is not permanent.
Living sacrifice, government, the weak brother, and a long list of names.

chapters.1: The theme stated: the just shall live by faith. Then the case that the invisible things of God are clearly seen, so the world is without excuse.
chapters.2: Turned on the moralist who agrees with chapter 1 — thou that judgest doest the same things. Circumcision is of the heart.
chapters.3: The charge concluded: there is none righteous, no, not one. Then the turn — justified freely by his grace, through the redemption in Christ.
chapters.4: Abraham as the test case. He was counted righteous in Genesis 15, before circumcision in Genesis 17, so faith cannot depend on it.
chapters.5: Being justified, we have peace. Suffering works patience. Adam and Christ set against each other as two heads of two humanities.
chapters.6: If grace abounds, shall we sin the more? Answered with baptism: dead to sin, buried with him, and not to live in it any longer.
chapters.7: The law is holy, but it names the sin it cannot cure. The wretched man who does what he hates — much argued over ever since.
chapters.8: No condemnation. The Spirit, adoption, the creation groaning, all things working together, and nothing able to separate us from the love of God.
chapters.9: The hardest three chapters begin. Election, the potter and the clay, and Paul's own wish that he were accursed for his kinsmen.
chapters.10: The word is nigh thee. Confession with the mouth and belief in the heart; how shall they hear without a preacher?
chapters.11: A remnant according to the election of grace. The olive tree with branches broken off and a wild branch grafted in, warned not to boast.
chapters.12: The turn to practice: present your bodies a living sacrifice. Gifts differing, love without dissimulation, and heaping coals of fire.
chapters.13: Be subject to the higher powers. Owe no man anything but to love; love is the fulfilling of the law.
chapters.14: The weak and the strong over meat and days. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind, and do not destroy him for whom Christ died.
chapters.15: Bearing the infirmities of the weak. Paul's plans — Jerusalem with the collection first, then Rome, then Spain.
chapters.16: Twenty-six people greeted by name, beginning with Phebe who probably carried the letter. Tertius the scribe adds his own greeting.

books.name: 1 Corinthians
books.full: The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians
books.scribe: Paul, with Sosthenes named as co-sender.
books.summary: A troubleshooting letter to a gifted, divided, morally chaotic church in a port city. Factions, a lawsuit, a sex scandal, disorderly worship, and confusion over resurrection — answered one at a time.
prophecies: 1 Cor 15:51–52 — we shall all be changed, at the last trump
laws: Guidance on marriage and singleness (7)
Order in worship and at the Lord's table (11–14)
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Factions answered with the foolishness of the cross.
A scandal, lawsuits between believers, and questions about singleness.
Rights surrendered for the sake of a weaker conscience.
Head coverings, the Lord's supper, spiritual gifts — and chapter 13 in the middle.
The fullest argument in scripture, then the collection and greetings.

chapters.1: Reports of quarrelling — I am of Paul, I of Apollos. The preaching of the cross set against Greek wisdom and Jewish signs.
chapters.2: I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified. Wisdom taught by the Spirit rather than by rhetoric.
chapters.3: Ye are yet carnal. Planting and watering, and the foundation on which men build gold or stubble, tried by fire.
chapters.4: Stewards of the mysteries. Paul's sarcasm about the Corinthians reigning as kings while the apostles are made a spectacle.
chapters.5: A case of incest the church is proud of tolerating. A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump; the man is to be handed over.
chapters.6: Believers suing one another before unbelievers. Then the body as the temple of the Holy Ghost: ye are not your own.
chapters.7: Answers on marriage, singleness and mixed marriages, with Paul carefully distinguishing what the Lord commands from his own judgment.
chapters.8: Meat offered to idols. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth — the weaker conscience outranks the stronger argument.
chapters.9: Paul's rights as an apostle, and why he waives them. I am made all things to all men. The runner and the boxer.
chapters.10: Israel in the wilderness as a warning. Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. Whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
chapters.11: Head coverings, then the Lord's supper abused at their common meals — one is hungry, and another is drunken.
chapters.12: Spiritual gifts, and the body with many members. The eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee.
chapters.13: The chapter on charity, placed deliberately in the middle of the argument about gifts. It suffereth long, and is kind; and it never faileth.
chapters.14: Prophecy preferred to tongues because it builds others up. Let all things be done decently and in order.
chapters.15: The resurrection: the earliest written account of the appearances, then the argument that if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain.
chapters.16: The collection to be laid by on the first day of the week, travel plans, and greetings. Quit you like men, be strong.

books.name: 2 Corinthians
books.full: The Second Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians
books.scribe: Paul, with Timothy as co-sender — his most personal and least guarded letter.
books.summary: Paul defends his ministry against rivals who called him unimpressive in person. He answers by listing not his successes but his beatings, shipwrecks and sleepless nights.
themes: Weakness as the place of power
laws: Principles of giving — willingly, proportionally, cheerfully (8–9)
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Comfort in affliction, the treasure in earthen vessels, the ministry of reconciliation.
Two chapters on giving for the poor in Jerusalem.
Paul's credentials: beatings, shipwrecks, a thorn, and grace sufficient.

chapters.1: The God of all comfort, who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble.
chapters.2: The offender is to be forgiven now, lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. We are unto God a sweet savour of Christ.
chapters.3: Ye are our epistle, written in fleshy tables of the heart. The veil on Moses' face, and the greater glory of the new covenant.
chapters.4: This treasure in earthen vessels. Troubled on every side, yet not distressed; cast down, but not destroyed.
chapters.5: The earthly house of this tabernacle dissolved. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature. We are ambassadors for Christ.
chapters.6: Now is the accepted time. A catalogue of hardships — as dying, and behold, we live; as poor, yet making many rich.
chapters.7: Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation, but the sorrow of the world worketh death. Titus brings good news from Corinth.
chapters.8: The Macedonians gave beyond their power. The collection urged, with careful arrangements so no one can question the handling of it.
chapters.9: God loveth a cheerful giver. He that soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly.
chapters.10: Paul answers the charge that his letters are weighty but his bodily presence weak. He will not compare himself with those who measure themselves by themselves.
chapters.11: The fool's speech begins. A list of what he has suffered — shipwrecks, stripes, perils — offered as reluctant credentials.
chapters.12: A man caught up to the third heaven, then the thorn in the flesh: my grace is sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in weakness.
chapters.13: Examine yourselves. A third visit threatened, and the closing benediction naming Father, Son and Spirit together.

books.name: Galatians
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Galatians
books.scribe: Paul — who notes in 6:11 that he has taken the pen from the scribe to write the ending in his own large hand.
books.summary: The angriest letter in the New Testament, and the only one with no thanksgiving. Teachers had arrived telling Gentile converts they must be circumcised; Paul treats this as a different gospel altogether.
laws: Gal 5:14 — all the law is fulfilled in one word: love thy neighbour as thyself
books.captivity: None.

moves.n: Called by no man; a confrontation with Peter at Antioch.
Abraham believed God — the law came 430 years later.
Stand fast in liberty; the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit.

chapters.1: No thanksgiving — straight to I marvel that ye are so soon removed. Paul insists his gospel came by revelation, not from Jerusalem.
chapters.2: Fourteen years later at Jerusalem, then the confrontation at Antioch where he withstood Peter to the face for withdrawing from Gentiles.
chapters.3: O foolish Galatians. Abraham believed God before the law existed; the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ.
chapters.4: Sons rather than servants, crying Abba, Father. Then the allegory of Hagar and Sarah, the two covenants.
chapters.5: Stand fast in the liberty. The works of the flesh listed against the fruit of the Spirit, which is singular: love, joy, peace.
chapters.6: Bear ye one another's burdens, and yet every man shall bear his own burden. Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.

books.name: Ephesians
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Ephesians
books.scribe: Paul, a prisoner — likely a circular letter, since the words 'at Ephesus' are missing from the earliest manuscripts.
books.summary: Three chapters on what is true, three on how to live in it. Written by a man in chains about a church described as seated in heavenly places.
laws: Household order — husbands, wives, children, servants (5:22–6:9)
books.captivity: Paul is himself in Roman custody.

moves.n: Chosen, redeemed, sealed; two walls made one; the mystery revealed.
Unity, new self, household order, and the whole armour of God.

chapters.1: One long sentence of blessing in the Greek, on election, redemption and the inheritance, sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.
chapters.2: Dead in trespasses, quickened together with Christ. By grace are ye saved through faith. The middle wall of partition broken down.
chapters.3: The mystery made known: Gentiles as fellowheirs. A prayer to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge.
chapters.4: One body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Then the practical turn — put off the old man, and let not the sun go down upon your wrath.
chapters.5: Walk in love. Be filled with the Spirit. Wives and husbands, with marriage set against the union of Christ and the church.
chapters.6: Children, parents, servants and masters. Then the whole armour of God, piece by piece, and prayer as the thing that holds it together.

books.name: Philippians
books.full: The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Philippians
books.scribe: Paul and Timothy, to the first church he planted in Europe.
books.summary: A thank-you letter for a financial gift that turns into a meditation on joy, written from a cell. It contains the hymn of Christ emptying himself.
books.captivity: Written in chains, with greetings from Caesar's household.

moves.n: Thanksgiving from prison; to me to live is Christ.
He made himself of no reputation — and God hath highly exalted him.
Paul's résumé counted as dung; pressing toward the mark.
Rejoice always; I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.

chapters.1: Written from prison, and the imprisonment has turned out to further the gospel. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
chapters.2: Let this mind be in you — he made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant. Timothy and Epaphroditus commended.
chapters.3: What things were gain to me, those I counted loss. Forgetting those things which are behind, I press toward the mark.
